name: Mind, Society & Philosophy
tagline: Thinking clearly about people, minds and what matters.

nodes.title: Feelings
nodes.goal: Name feelings and notice them in others.
nodes.kid_text: Feelings are the way your heart tells you what is happening inside. When your tummy feels warm and light, that is happy; when tears come, that is sad. Look at your friend's face: if their mouth turns down and their eyes get wet, they might feel sad too. You can ask, 'Are you okay?' and give them a hug.

quiz.prompt: Which face is happy?
quiz.say: Look at the three faces. Which one looks happy — the smiling face 😀, the crying face 😢, or the angry face 😠?
quiz.explain: A big smile and bright eyes mean somebody feels happy.

quiz.prompt: Tears and a frown. Feeling?
choices: sad
happy
silly
quiz.answer: sad
quiz.say: Your friend has tears in her eyes and her mouth turns down. Does she feel sad, happy, or silly?
quiz.explain: Tears and a turned-down mouth usually mean someone feels sad.

quiz.prompt: Friend is sad. What helps? 🧒
choices: hug
laugh
run
quiz.answer: hug
quiz.say: Your friend feels sad. What helps him most? A hug, a laugh at him, or a run away?
quiz.explain: A gentle hug and asking 'Are you okay?' help a sad friend feel better.

quiz.prompt: Big present 🎁 for you. You feel?
choices: scared
excited
sleepy
quiz.answer: excited
quiz.say: Someone hands you a big present with a bow on top. Do you feel scared, excited, or sleepy?
quiz.explain: That jumpy, happy feeling inside is called excited.

quiz.prompt: Someone grabs your toy 🧸. You feel?
choices: angry
proud
sleepy
quiz.answer: angry
quiz.say: Somebody grabs your toy right out of your hands. Do you feel angry, proud, or sleepy?
quiz.explain: That hot, stompy feeling when something is unfair is anger.

quiz.prompt: Wide eyes, open mouth. Feeling?
choices: surprised
bored
angry
quiz.answer: surprised
quiz.say: Your friend's eyes go wide and her mouth pops open. Does she feel surprised, bored, or angry?
quiz.explain: Wide eyes and an open mouth mean somebody feels surprised.

quiz.prompt: Not sure how she feels. Do what?
choices: ask her
walk away
shout
quiz.answer: ask her
quiz.say: Your friend looks a bit funny and you are not sure how she feels. Do you ask her, walk away, or shout?
quiz.explain: Asking 'Are you okay?' is the kindest way to find out.

lesson_media.alt: Two children enter the same new school: Sam notices a fast heartbeat and worries about getting lost, while Lee feels wide-eyed excitement; each names a feeling and chooses a different helpful response.
lesson_media.caption: Feelings involve situations, body clues and interpretations. The same event can feel different to different people, so empathy begins by noticing and asking.

nodes.title: Fair and Kind
nodes.goal: Share, take turns and be kind.
nodes.kid_text: Being fair means everyone gets a turn, not just you. If you have one red truck and a friend wants to play, you can share it or take turns counting to ten. Kind words like 'please,' 'thank you,' and 'you can go first' make people feel warm inside. When you share, playing is more fun for everybody.

quiz.prompt: One swing 🛝, two kids. Do what?
choices: take turns
grab it
push
quiz.answer: take turns
quiz.say: There is one swing and two children who want it. Do you take turns, grab it, or push?
quiz.explain: Taking turns means everybody gets a go, and that is fair.

quiz.prompt: Which word is kind?
choices: please
go away
mine
quiz.answer: please
quiz.say: Which of these words is a kind word? Please, go away, or mine?
quiz.explain: Kind words like please and thank you make people feel warm inside.

quiz.prompt: 🍪🍪🍪🍪 shared by two kids. Each gets?
quiz.say: Here are four cookies to share between two children. How many does each child get? Is it 1, 2, or 4?
quiz.explain: Two cookies each — the same for everyone, so it is fair.

quiz.prompt: 🍇🍇🍇🍇🍇🍇🍇🍇🍇 shared by three kids. Each gets?
quiz.say: Nine grapes are shared fairly between three children. How many does each one get? Is it 2, 3, or 6?
quiz.explain: Nine grapes split three ways is three each, and three each is fair.

quiz.prompt: Friend drops her blocks 🧱. Kind thing?
choices: help her
just watch
laugh
quiz.answer: help her
quiz.say: Your friend drops all her blocks on the floor. Do you help her, just watch, or laugh?
quiz.explain: Helping is a kind thing, and it makes your friend feel warm inside.

quiz.prompt: Someone gives you a gift 🎁. Say?
choices: thank you
gimme more
nothing
quiz.answer: thank you
quiz.say: Grandma gives you a little gift. Do you say thank you, say gimme more, or say nothing?
quiz.explain: Thank you is a kind word that makes people feel happy.

quiz.prompt: You had the first turn. Now who?
choices: me again
my friend
nobody
quiz.answer: my friend
quiz.say: You already had the first turn on the trike. Who goes next — me again, my friend, or nobody?
quiz.explain: After your turn it is somebody else's turn. That is taking turns.

lesson_media.alt: Three worked panels distinguish equal sharing of one box each, equitable support using boxes of different heights to overcome a barrier, and timed turns on one shared bicycle.
lesson_media.caption: Fair can mean equal shares, relevant support or turns depending on the problem. Kindness attends to how the arrangement affects actual people.

nodes.title: Making Choices
nodes.goal: Choose and say why.
nodes.kid_text: A choice is when you pick one thing instead of another, like an apple or a banana for snack. Before you pick, think about which one you really want and why. Then you can say, 'I want the apple because it is crunchy!' Saying your reason helps other people understand you.

quiz.prompt: Which word tells why?
choices: because
and
the
quiz.answer: because
quiz.say: When you tell someone why you picked something, which word do you use? Because, and, or the?
quiz.explain: The word 'because' tells everyone the reason for your choice.

quiz.prompt: A choice means you pick...
choices: one
all
none
quiz.answer: one
quiz.say: When you make a choice, do you pick one thing, all the things, or none of them?
quiz.explain: A choice means picking one thing instead of another.

quiz.prompt: Snow ❄️. Why pick a coat? 🧥
choices: it is cold
it is yummy
it is loud
quiz.answer: it is cold
quiz.say: It is snowy outside, so you choose a big warm coat. Is that because it is cold, it is yummy, or it is loud?
quiz.explain: A good reason matches what you really noticed — snow is cold!

quiz.prompt: You are very thirsty 🏃. Choose?
choices: water
a hat
a book
quiz.answer: water
quiz.say: You are very thirsty after running. Do you choose water, a hat, or a book?
quiz.explain: Good choosing means picking the thing that fits what you need.

quiz.prompt: Hot sunny day ☀️. Why a hat? 🧢
choices: shade
noisy
yummy
quiz.answer: shade
quiz.say: It is a hot sunny day, so you pick a hat. Is that for shade, because it is noisy, or because it is yummy?
quiz.explain: A good reason matches what you noticed — the sun is bright and hot!

quiz.prompt: Nobody knows why you picked it. Do?
choices: tell them
hide it
shrug
quiz.answer: tell them
quiz.say: Your friends do not know why you picked the blue cup. Do you tell them, hide it, or shrug?
quiz.explain: Saying your reason helps other people understand you.

quiz.prompt: Before you pick, first you should?
choices: think
shout
hurry
quiz.answer: think
quiz.say: Before you choose your snack, what is best to do first? Think, shout, or hurry?
quiz.explain: Thinking first helps you pick what you really want.

lesson_media.alt: A two-by-two decision table compares taking an umbrella or leaving it behind under two uncertain outcomes, rain or dry weather, and lists the consequence of each choice-outcome pair.
lesson_media.caption: A reason connects what matters and what we know to a choice. Uncertainty means a good decision can still have an unlucky result.

nodes.title: Good Thinking
nodes.goal: Ask questions; give reasons for what you believe.
nodes.kid_text: Good thinking starts with a question, like 'Why is the sky blue?' or 'How does a bird fly?' When you say what you believe, give a reason so people know why you think it. If you say 'I think it will rain,' you can add 'because the clouds are dark and gray.' A reason is like a rope that ties your idea to something you noticed.

quiz.prompt: Which word starts a question? ❓
choices: Why
Yes
Blue
quiz.answer: Why
quiz.say: Which of these words starts a question? Why, yes, or blue?
quiz.explain: Words like why, how and what are how questions begin.

quiz.prompt: Dark gray clouds ☁️. What is likely?
choices: rain is coming
it will stay dry
the sun will burn hot
quiz.answer: rain is coming
quiz.say: The clouds outside are dark and gray. What is most likely — rain is coming, it will stay dry, or the sun will burn hot?
quiz.explain: Dark gray clouds are a real clue, so that is a good reason to say rain.

quiz.prompt: Dog is happy 🐕. How do you know?
choices: its tail wags
just because
dogs are always happy
quiz.answer: its tail wags
quiz.say: You say the dog feels happy. How do you know? Its tail wags, just because, or dogs are always happy?
quiz.explain: A good reason points to something you really saw, like a wagging tail.

quiz.prompt: Puddles all over the path 🚶. Why?
choices: it rained
the sun shone
it was windy
quiz.answer: it rained
quiz.say: You see puddles all over the path this morning. Is that because it rained, the sun shone, or it was windy?
quiz.explain: Puddles are a clue, and rain is the reason that fits the clue.

quiz.prompt: Milk is gone. Which is a reason?
choices: I saw the empty jug
just because
I always say so
quiz.answer: I saw the empty jug
quiz.say: You say the milk is all gone. Which is a real reason — I saw the empty jug, just because, or I always say so?
quiz.explain: A real reason points at something you actually noticed.

quiz.prompt: You wonder about stars ⭐. Best start?
choices: ask a question
take a nap
guess an answer
quiz.answer: ask a question
quiz.say: You really want to know why stars twinkle. Do you ask a question, take a nap, or guess an answer?
quiz.explain: Good thinking always starts with a question.

quiz.prompt: No clue at all. That is a?
choices: guess
good reason
proof
quiz.answer: guess
quiz.say: You say something but you have no clue at all to back it up. Is that a guess, a good reason, or proof?
quiz.explain: With no clue it is only a guess — good thinking needs a reason.

lesson_media.alt: A four-step argument begins with the claim that a plant grew taller because it was near a window, adds a measured example, asks whether water or plant type also differed, and proposes a fair comparison to test the reason.
lesson_media.caption: Good thinking makes a claim, gives a relevant reason, checks evidence and asks what else could explain the result.

nodes.title: Getting Along
nodes.goal: Friendship, cooperation and resolving conflict.
nodes.kid_text: Friends are people you like to be with, and being a good friend means helping and taking turns. Sometimes friends disagree, like when you both want the same swing. Instead of grabbing or yelling, you can use your words: 'Can I have a turn next?' Working together, like building one big tower, is more fun than fighting.

quiz.prompt: Both want the swing 🛝. Best?
choices: ask
grab
yell
quiz.answer: ask
quiz.say: You and your friend both want the same swing. What works best? Ask with words, grab it, or yell?
quiz.explain: Using words like 'Can I have a turn next?' keeps friends happy.

quiz.prompt: One big tower 🧱, two friends. Best?
choices: build it together
each build alone
knock it down
quiz.answer: build it together
quiz.say: You and your friend both want one really big tower. Do you build it together, each build alone, or knock it down?
quiz.explain: Working together makes big jobs easier and more fun.

quiz.prompt: You bumped a friend. Say?
choices: sorry
nothing
you moved!
quiz.answer: sorry
quiz.say: You bumped into your friend by accident and she dropped her blocks. Do you say sorry, say nothing, or say you moved?
quiz.explain: Saying sorry helps a friend feel better again fast.

quiz.prompt: Girl stands alone 😔. You do?
choices: invite her
ignore her
laugh
quiz.answer: invite her
quiz.say: A girl is standing all alone with nobody to play with. Do you invite her, ignore her, or laugh?
quiz.explain: Inviting someone in is what a good friend does.

quiz.prompt: Friend wants a different game 🎲. Best?
choices: take turns
play only mine
stop playing
quiz.answer: take turns
quiz.say: You want tag but your friend wants a board game. Do you take turns, play only mine, or stop playing?
quiz.explain: Taking turns with ideas means both friends get a happy turn.

quiz.prompt: Friend won the race 🏃. You say?
choices: good job
cheater!
not fair
quiz.answer: good job
quiz.say: Your friend won the race and you came second. Do you say good job, shout cheater, or say not fair?
quiz.explain: Being a good sport keeps friends close even when you lose.

quiz.prompt: Friend says sorry 🙂. You then?
choices: forgive her
stay cross
never play again
quiz.answer: forgive her
quiz.say: Your friend says sorry for knocking down your tower. Do you forgive her, stay cross, or never play again?
quiz.explain: Forgiving lets you both get back to playing together.

lesson_media.alt: A five-step playground conflict process moves from pausing, hearing each person's account, paraphrasing the other view, naming both needs and proposing a testable agreement about sharing a game.
lesson_media.caption: Resolving conflict does not require pretending everyone saw the event alike. Listening, restating and naming needs create room for a workable repair.

nodes.title: Money Sense
nodes.goal: Earning, saving, spending and giving.
nodes.kid_text: Money is what people trade for things they need, like food or a toy. You can earn money by helping, save it in a piggy bank to buy something bigger later, or spend it now on something small. Saving means waiting, and waiting can get you a bigger treat. It feels good to give some too, like helping someone who has less.

quiz.prompt: You wash the car 🚗 for coins. That is?
choices: earning
giving
saving
quiz.answer: earning
quiz.say: You helped wash the car and got some coins for it. Is that earning, giving, or saving?
quiz.explain: Doing helpful work and getting money for it is called earning.

quiz.prompt: How many coins? 🪙🪙🪙🪙🪙
quiz.say: Count the coins in the piggy bank with me. Are there 3, 4, or 5?
quiz.explain: Five coins! Counting your money tells you what you can buy.

quiz.prompt: Coins stay in the piggy 🐷. That is?
choices: saving
spending
earning
quiz.answer: saving
quiz.say: You keep your coins in the piggy bank to buy something bigger later. Is that saving, spending, or earning?
quiz.explain: Keeping money for later is saving, and waiting can get you something bigger.

quiz.prompt: You buy an ice cream 🍦. That is?
choices: spending
earning
saving
quiz.answer: spending
quiz.say: You hand over your coins and get an ice cream. Is that spending, earning, or saving?
quiz.explain: Swapping your money for something is called spending.

quiz.prompt: Coins to a kid with none 🤝. That is?
choices: giving
saving
earning
quiz.answer: giving
quiz.say: You hand some of your coins to a child who has none. Is that giving, saving, or earning?
quiz.explain: Sharing money with someone who has less is called giving.

quiz.prompt: Toy costs 5 🪙. You have 3. Do?
choices: save more coins
buy it today
ask for a bigger toy
quiz.answer: save more coins
quiz.say: The toy costs five coins but you only have three. Do you save more coins, buy it today, or ask for a bigger toy?
quiz.explain: Three is less than five, so you need to save two more coins.

quiz.prompt: Want a big kite 🪁 later. Do?
choices: save
spend now
give it away
quiz.answer: save
quiz.say: You really want a big kite that costs lots of coins. Do you save, spend now, or give it away?
quiz.explain: Saving means waiting, and waiting can get you something bigger.

lesson_media.alt: Ten one-dollar coins are grouped into a balanced example budget: five dollars for needs, three to save, one to give and one for wants, with the arithmetic five plus three plus one plus one equals ten.
lesson_media.caption: A budget assigns limited money among present needs, future goals, giving and optional wants. Real categories and amounts depend on a person's circumstances.

nodes.title: Right and Wrong
nodes.goal: Think about what is fair and why rules help.
nodes.kid_text: Rules are agreements that help everyone stay safe and be treated fairly. A good way to know what is right is to ask, 'Would I want someone to do this to me?' If you would not like being pushed, then pushing others is not fair. Rules like 'take turns' and 'be gentle' help everyone play happily together.

quiz.prompt: Rules help everyone stay...
choices: safe
hungry
bored
quiz.answer: safe
quiz.say: Why do we have rules like 'be gentle'? To help everyone stay safe, hungry, or bored?
quiz.explain: Rules keep us safe and make sure everyone is treated fairly.

quiz.prompt: You hate being pushed. Pushing others is?
choices: not fair
fine
funny
quiz.answer: not fair
quiz.say: You would not like it if someone pushed you. So is pushing someone else not fair, fine, or funny?
quiz.explain: If you would not want it done to you, it is not fair to do it to others.

quiz.prompt: Line at the slide 🛝. Do what?
choices: wait your turn
push in
go home
quiz.answer: wait your turn
quiz.say: There is a line of children at the slide. Do you wait your turn, push in, or go home?
quiz.explain: Waiting your turn is the fair rule, and it works for everybody.

quiz.prompt: Rolls 3, moves 8 spaces 🎲. That is?
choices: cheating
winning
lucky
quiz.answer: cheating
quiz.say: In the board game your friend rolls a three but moves eight spaces. Is that cheating, winning, or lucky?
quiz.explain: Breaking the rules is cheating, and it makes the game unfair.

quiz.prompt: It feels nice when others give you some. So?
choices: share
hide it
take more
quiz.answer: share
quiz.say: It feels lovely when somebody gives you some of their snack. So what do you do with yours? Share, hide it, or take more?
quiz.explain: Treat other people the way you would like to be treated.

quiz.prompt: You broke the cup 🥤. You say?
choices: it was me
the cat did it
nothing
quiz.answer: it was me
quiz.say: You knocked over the cup and it broke. Do you say it was me, the cat did it, or nothing?
quiz.explain: Telling the truth is the right thing, even when it feels hard.

quiz.prompt: No road rules at all 🚗. Then?
choices: crashes
safe roads
quiet roads
quiz.answer: crashes
quiz.say: Imagine cars with no road rules at all. Would there be crashes, safe roads, or quiet roads?
quiz.explain: Rules stop crashes and keep everybody safe.

lesson_media.alt: A four-step ethics check starts with cutting a lunch line, asks what happens if everyone does it, checks harm, consent and fairness, and revises the action to waiting or asking for an agreed exception.
lesson_media.caption: Rules help coordinate people when their actions affect one another. A reasoned rule considers general use, harm, consent, fairness and justified exceptions.

nodes.title: Logic and Puzzles
nodes.goal: Valid reasoning; spotting bad arguments.

lesson_media.alt: Within a large wooden rectangular tray, four square tiles sit inside a smaller brass-outlined group while one tall non-square rectangle remains in the tray outside that group.
lesson_media.caption: Every square is a rectangle, but the tall rectangle is a counterexample to the reversed claim that every rectangle is a square.

lesson_media.title: Test the reverse
lesson_media.instructions: Start with the true statement that every square is a rectangle. Reverse it, then reveal the rectangle that disproves the reverse.

quiz.prompt: Maria says: 'All dogs are animals. My pet Rex is an animal. So Rex is a dog.' Even though her sentences sound reasonable, her conclusion is not guaranteed. Why?
quiz.answer: Many animals are not dogs, so being an animal cannot prove that Rex is a dog.
quiz.explain: The premise puts every dog inside the larger group of animals, but it does not say that every animal is a dog. Rex could be another kind of animal.
choices: The name Rex is not specific enough to pick out any one particular animal.
All animals are dogs, so her argument is correct after all.
Many animals are not dogs, so being an animal cannot prove that Rex is a dog.
You cannot know anything at all about Rex unless you go and see him.

quiz.prompt: In a debate, Sam cannot answer Priya's point, so instead he says, 'Well, Priya has messy hair, so nobody should listen to her.' What is wrong with Sam's response?
quiz.answer: He attacks the person instead of answering the actual argument.
quiz.explain: Insulting a person rather than addressing their reasoning is a fallacy and does not show the argument is wrong.
choices: He gives far too many separate reasons all at the very same time.
He accidentally agrees with Priya without noticing that he has.
He is correct, since untidy hair shows that someone must be wrong.
He attacks the person instead of answering the actual argument.

quiz.prompt: A poster says: 'Either you love our town's football team, or you hate our town.' Ana likes the team a little but does not think much about football. What is wrong with the poster's reasoning?
quiz.answer: It offers only two choices when others exist.
choices: It uses the word 'hate', which is a very strong word to put on a poster.
It is right, because a person has to pick one of the two sides given.
It offers only two choices when others exist.
It talks about football, and football is not the same thing as a town.
quiz.explain: This is a false dilemma: the poster pretends there are only two options when plenty of in-between positions are possible.

quiz.prompt: Ben says: 'Every bird I have seen in my garden is brown. So every bird in the world must be brown.' What is the quickest way to show Ben he is wrong?
quiz.answer: Show him one bird that is not brown, such as a bright red cardinal.
choices: Count the brown birds in his garden again, much more carefully this time.
Tell him that gardens are quite small places.
Ask him how many hours he watched the birds.
Show him one bird that is not brown, such as a bright red cardinal.
quiz.explain: A claim about every bird is knocked down by a single counterexample, which is why one non-brown bird settles it.

quiz.prompt: Rafi says: 'All squares are rectangles, so all rectangles are squares.' Explain why turning the sentence around breaks the reasoning.
quiz.answer: A rectangle is a four-sided shape with four right angles, while a square must also have four equal sides; a long thin rectangle is a counterexample to the reversed claim.
quiz.explain: 'All A are B' does not give you 'all B are A'. Every square is a four-sided shape with four right angles, so it is a rectangle; some rectangles have unequal side lengths, so they are not squares.

quiz.prompt: A sign says: 'If it is raining, the flag is taken down.' Today the flag is down. Kaya decides it must be raining. Why might Kaya be wrong?
quiz.answer: The flag may be taken down for other reasons too.
choices: Flags cannot be seen in the rain.
The flag may be taken down for other reasons too.
The sign was written about yesterday, not about today at all.
Rain does not actually cause anybody to take a flag down.
quiz.explain: The sign promises the flag comes down when it rains, not that rain is the only thing that brings it down.

quiz.prompt: A rule says: 'If someone is a member, then that person may enter the pool.' The rule gives no other information. Rio is not a member. What follows about Rio?
quiz.answer: Nothing certain follows from the rule
choices: Nothing certain follows from the rule
Rio may not enter the pool
Rio is already in the pool
Rio will become a member soon
quiz.explain: The rule tells you what follows from being a member. It gives no rule for non-members, so Rio's case remains open. Negating a one-way rule adds information that the rule never stated.

quiz.prompt: In a group of 20 children, 12 play football, 9 play chess, and 5 play both. How many play neither game?
quiz.explain: 12 + 9 = 21, but the 5 who play both were counted twice, so 21 - 5 = 16 play at least one. That leaves 20 - 16 = 4.

quiz.prompt: Ana argues: 'The last three times I forgot my umbrella it rained, so forgetting my umbrella makes it rain.' Which question best shows the trouble with her reasoning?
quiz.answer: How often did it rain on the days she remembered it?
choices: How often did it rain on the days she remembered it?
How heavy was the rain on each of those days?
Did she buy the umbrella herself?
Was the umbrella big enough for two people?
quiz.explain: To test whether one thing affects another you have to look at the cases where it did not happen too. Counting only the hits will confirm almost anything.

quiz.prompt: Tom says: 'Nobody I know has seen a green cat, so green cats do not exist.' Explain what would settle the question, and why Tom's reason is weak.
quiz.answer: One clear example of a green cat would settle it; Tom's reason is weak because his friends have searched a tiny part of the world, so not seeing something is thin evidence that it is not there.
quiz.explain: Absence of evidence is only strong evidence of absence when you have actually looked hard in the right places.

nodes.title: How the Mind Works
nodes.goal: Memory, attention and learning.

quiz.prompt: You are trying to memorize a list of 12 spelling words, but you keep getting distracted by a loud TV. Based on how attention and memory work, what should you do to remember them best?
quiz.answer: Turn off the TV and practice the words in short sessions across several days.
quiz.explain: Removing distractions frees your attention, and spreading practice across days helps memory far more than one long crammed session.
choices: Stare at the list for one full hour straight on the night before the big test.
Say the words only inside your head while watching your favorite TV show.
Turn off the TV and practice the words in short sessions across several days.
Read the whole list once with the TV on and trust that you will remember.

quiz.prompt: A child learns to ride a bike after falling many times, and soon can ride without thinking about it. Which idea best explains what happened?
quiz.answer: Learning: practice changed her behavior so the skill became automatic.
quiz.explain: Learning is a lasting change in behavior from experience, and repeated practice can make a skill automatic.
choices: Attention: her focus narrowed so far that she noticed nothing else at all.
Learning: practice changed her behavior so the skill became automatic.
Instinct: she was born knowing how to ride and simply recalled it.
Memory: her recollection of each fall was erased right after every attempt.

quiz.prompt: A memory experiment shows a class a list of 20 words one time. Priya later recalls 14 of them. How many of the words did she fail to recall?
quiz.explain: 20 words shown minus 14 recalled leaves 6 that she did not recall.

quiz.prompt: Ravi reads his history notes while texting a friend at the same time. The next day he remembers almost nothing from the notes. What best explains this?
quiz.answer: His attention was split, so little was stored.
choices: His memory was already full, so no new facts could fit inside it.
Texting tires out the eyes, which wipes away memories already stored.
Notes written by hand are harder to recall than typed-up notes.
His attention was split, so little was stored.
quiz.explain: Attention is limited. Splitting it between two tasks means the material is barely encoded, so there is little to recall later.

quiz.prompt: A magician asks the audience to watch a coin in her right hand while she quietly hides a ball with her left. Hardly anyone sees the left hand move. Which idea about attention does the trick use?
quiz.answer: Attention works like a spotlight
choices: People forget what they saw after a few minutes.
Eyes are unable to see anything that moves quickly.
The left hand is harder to see than the right hand.
Attention works like a spotlight
quiz.explain: So what falls outside it often goes unnoticed. Attention lights up one part of a scene at a time, and events outside that spotlight can pass by without being noticed at all.

quiz.prompt: Ten minutes after hearing a new phone number, Yusuf can still say it. Two days later it is gone. Yet he can still ride a bike after a whole winter of not riding. What does this difference show?
quiz.answer: Some memories fade fast while skills last much longer.
choices: Bikes are easier than numbers.
Some memories fade fast while skills last much longer.
Phone numbers are stored in the legs rather than in the brain.
Anything a person learns on a weekend is forgotten by the next week.
quiz.explain: A number held briefly sits in short-term memory, while a practised skill like cycling is stored in a longer-lasting memory system.

quiz.prompt: A teacher reads out a list of ten words, and most children remember the first two and the last two best. Which explanation fits that pattern?
quiz.answer: The start and end of a list are easier to recall than the middle
choices: The start and end of a list are easier to recall than the middle
The middle words were spoken more quietly
Short words are remembered better than long ones
The children stopped paying attention right at the start of the list
quiz.explain: Psychologists call this the serial position effect. The first items get more rehearsal and the last are still fresh, so the middle suffers.

quiz.prompt: Ana practises the piano for 20 minutes a day on each of 5 days, then 40 minutes on the sixth day. How many minutes has she practised altogether?
quiz.explain: 5 x 20 = 100, plus 40 = 140 minutes. Spread over six days, that practice sticks far better than 140 minutes in one sitting.

quiz.prompt: Sam can name every capital city but cannot say how he learned them. Nina can ride a bike but cannot explain how she does it. What best captures the difference between what they know?
quiz.answer: One kind of knowing can be told; the other is shown by doing
choices: One kind of knowing can be told; the other is shown by doing
Nina's knowledge is stored for a shorter time
Sam pays better attention than Nina does
Riding a bike uses no memory at all
quiz.explain: Facts you can state and skills you can perform are stored differently in the brain, which is why someone can lose one and keep the other.

quiz.prompt: A student learns a poem by heart on Monday and says it perfectly. By Friday most of it has gone. What would have been the best way to keep it?
quiz.answer: Try to recall it from memory for a minute on each day in between
choices: Try to recall it from memory for a minute on each day in between
Read the poem through carefully once more on the Thursday night before
Copy the whole poem out very neatly into a fresh notebook on Monday
Learn a second poem at the same time
quiz.explain: Pulling something out of memory strengthens it much more than putting it in again. Doing that on several days beats one long effort.

lesson_media.alt: A five-step arrow path runs from sights and sounds through selective attention, limited working memory, active encoding and practice, and retrieval from long-term memory.
lesson_media.caption: Learning is not a camera recording. Attention selects, working memory transforms a small amount, and retrieval practice makes long-term access more durable.

nodes.title: Living Together
nodes.goal: Cultures, communities and society.

quiz.prompt: A family moves from one country to another and finds that people greet each other with a bow instead of a handshake, and eat different foods. This difference in customs, food, and greetings is best described as a difference in what?
quiz.answer: Culture
quiz.explain: Culture is the shared customs, foods, language, and ways of doing things that a group of people passes along.
choices: Weather
Government building
Population
Culture

quiz.prompt: A scientist wants to understand why people in a town formed a club to clean the river together. Which field of study is she most directly using?
quiz.answer: Sociology, the study of how people act together in groups.
quiz.explain: Sociology studies how people form groups, cooperate, and behave in society, which fits studying a community cleanup club.
choices: Astronomy, the study of the stars and the distant planets.
Geology, the study of rocks and how they slowly form.
Sociology, the study of how people act together in groups.
Botany, the study of plants and how they grow and spread.

quiz.prompt: Your school has a rule that everyone lines up before entering the classroom. Give one reason a group of people might agree to a rule like this, even though it slows each person down.
quiz.answer: A shared rule keeps the group orderly and fair, so nobody is pushed aside and everyone gets a turn.
quiz.explain: Rules trade a small cost for each person against a benefit for the group: order, fairness, and fewer arguments.

quiz.prompt: A town builds a library that anybody may use free of charge, paid for by taxes that townspeople pay together. What is the best name for something paid for together and used by everyone?
quiz.answer: A public good.
choices: A private business, run in order to make a profit.
A charity.
A public good.
A prize, won by the best student in the town.
quiz.explain: A public good is funded collectively and open to all, rather than sold to one buyer at a time.

quiz.prompt: A family moves to a new neighborhood and is surprised that neighbors leave their shoes by the front door. Nobody has written this rule down, yet people follow it. What is this kind of unwritten rule called?
quiz.answer: A social norm
choices: A law, written down and enforced by a court.
A hobby.
A wage, paid to someone for doing work.
A social norm
quiz.explain: A shared habit that a group expects people to follow. Social norms are unwritten expectations. Breaking one brings disapproval rather than legal punishment, which is what separates a norm from a law.

quiz.prompt: Two villages both need a bridge, but neither wants to pay for the whole thing alone. They agree to split the cost and share the bridge. This agreement is an example of what?
quiz.answer: Cooperation for a shared benefit.
choices: Competition between rivals.
Cooperation for a shared benefit.
Punishment for breaking an agreed rule.
Tradition handed down from grandparents to children.
quiz.explain: When a benefit is too costly for one party alone, groups often cooperate and share both the cost and the result.

quiz.prompt: A town has one park that anyone may use. Litter has become a problem, and each visitor thinks their own wrapper makes hardly any difference. Which idea does this best show?
quiz.answer: Shared things can be spoilt by many small choices
choices: Shared things can be spoilt by many small choices
People in towns care less than people in villages
Parks should close whenever they get dirty
Litter happens because there are too few bins
quiz.explain: When a cost is shared by everyone and the benefit is private, each small decision looks harmless while the total does the damage.

quiz.prompt: A village agrees that each household pays $6 towards a bridge. There are 120 households. How many dollars does the village raise?
quiz.explain: 120 x 6 = 720. Sharing a big cost across many people is how communities pay for things nobody could afford alone.

quiz.prompt: In one country people form a line at a bus stop; in another they wait in a group and board when the bus comes. Both systems work. What does that best show about customs?
quiz.answer: Different customs can solve the same problem
choices: Different customs can solve the same problem
People in one country are more polite than the other
Queueing is the natural human behaviour
Buses run better where people form lines
quiz.explain: Customs are agreed solutions, not laws of nature. Several different agreements can do the same job.

quiz.prompt: Your class collects money for a shared class pet, but two people refuse to pay and still enjoy the pet. Explain why this is a problem for the group, and give one fair way to handle it.
quiz.answer: If people can enjoy a shared thing without paying, others start to feel foolish for contributing and the class may not raise enough; a fair way is to agree the rule before buying, so the pet is bought only once everyone has contributed, or to let non-payers help with the work instead.
quiz.explain: This is the free-rider problem in miniature, and the usual answers are the same: agree the rule first, or accept a contribution in a different form.

lesson_media.alt: A reciprocal network links a school-day norm at the center to individuals, peer groups, cultural meanings and formal institutions, with two-way arrows showing people learn and also change social patterns.
lesson_media.caption: Society is neither only individuals nor an entity above them. People act through groups, meanings and institutions, reproducing or changing norms through feedback.

nodes.title: Big Questions
nodes.goal: What is real? What is fair? What is a good life?

quiz.prompt: Two friends argue about whether it is fair for the strongest kid to always pick the game everyone plays. They are not testing this with a science experiment but by thinking carefully about what 'fair' means. This kind of careful thinking about big ideas like fairness is called what?
quiz.answer: Philosophy
quiz.explain: Philosophy uses careful reasoning to explore big questions such as what is fair, what is real, and what is good.
choices: Gardening
Chemistry
Arithmetic
Philosophy

quiz.prompt: Someone who is wise does something different from someone who just knows a lot of facts. Which of these best shows wisdom rather than only knowledge?
quiz.answer: Using what you know about anger to stay calm in a real fight.
quiz.explain: Wisdom is using knowledge and good judgment to act well in real life, not just holding many facts.
choices: Winning a memory game by matching more cards than everyone.
Reciting every capital city in the entire world without pausing.
Naming all of the planets in order without making a single mistake.
Using what you know about anger to stay calm in a real fight.

quiz.prompt: A friend says, 'Nothing is real except what I can touch.' Name one thing that seems real but cannot be touched, and say why that makes his claim hard to defend.
quiz.answer: Numbers, or feelings such as sadness, cannot be touched yet clearly matter, so touching cannot be the test of what is real.
quiz.explain: Plenty of things we treat as real, such as numbers, feelings, and rules, are untouchable, so touch is a poor test of reality.

quiz.prompt: Ada asks, 'How do I know I am not dreaming right now?' Every test she can think of, such as pinching herself or checking a clock, could also happen inside a dream. What kind of question has she run into?
quiz.answer: A question about how we know things.
choices: A question about how many hours of sleep a child needs each night.
A question that a careful science experiment could easily settle.
A question about which sort of clock keeps the most accurate time.
A question about how we know things.
quiz.explain: She has stumbled onto a question of knowledge itself: what would count as good enough evidence, and can any test settle it?

quiz.prompt: Two children agree that stealing is wrong. One says it is wrong because it hurts people; the other says it is wrong because it breaks a promise everyone has made. What are they actually disagreeing about?
quiz.answer: Not whether stealing is wrong, but what makes it wrong.
choices: Whether the stealing really happened.
Whether people are allowed to promise things.
Whether being hurt is ever a pleasant feeling.
Not whether stealing is wrong, but what makes it wrong.
quiz.explain: They share the same verdict but offer different reasons for it, which is a disagreement about the grounds of the rule rather than the rule itself.

quiz.prompt: Someone says, 'A good life just means having as much fun as possible.' Which reply challenges that idea most directly?
quiz.answer: Some hard, unfun lives look admirable.
choices: Fun is hard to measure in units, so the claim tells us little.
Having fun costs money, and money is hard for many people to come by.
Some hard, unfun lives look admirable.
People disagree about which particular activities they find the most fun.
quiz.explain: Lives spent on difficult work, care, or training are widely admired, which suggests fun is not the whole of a good life.

quiz.prompt: Kai says a painting is beautiful and Ori says it is ugly, and neither of them is lying. Which reply takes the disagreement most seriously?
quiz.answer: They may be noticing different things in the painting
choices: They may be noticing different things in the painting
One of them must be mistaken about the facts
Beauty can be measured with an instrument
Whichever of them is older should decide
quiz.explain: Some disagreements are not about facts one side has wrong. Asking what each person is responding to often makes the disagreement useful.

quiz.prompt: A robot says 'I am sad' whenever its battery runs low. A child asks whether the robot really feels sad. Which question would help most in answering?
quiz.answer: What would count as evidence of feeling rather than of saying?
choices: What would count as evidence of feeling rather than of saying?
How loudly does the robot say the words when its battery runs low?
Who designed and built the robot, and in which year was it finished?
How long does the robot's battery last between one charge and the next?
quiz.explain: Before you can answer a hard question you often have to decide what an answer would look like. That step is doing philosophy.

quiz.prompt: Two people agree that helping a stranger is good, but they disagree about why. Why does that disagreement still matter?
quiz.answer: Their different reasons will give different answers in new cases
choices: Their different reasons will give different answers in new cases
One of them is not really helping anyone
Reasons matter less than results
Agreeing about the action makes reasons pointless
quiz.explain: Reasons are the part of a moral view that travels. Two people can agree today and split sharply the first time a hard case arrives.

quiz.prompt: A famous puzzle asks about a ship with 60 planks, one of which is replaced each year. After how many years does the ship contain none of its original planks?
quiz.explain: After 60 years every plank has been swapped. Philosophers then ask whether it is still the same ship, which is a question arithmetic cannot answer.

lesson_media.alt: Three columns apply consequence, rule and character or care lenses to the same question of whether to reveal a friend's harmful secret, naming what each lens notices and what evidence remains needed.
lesson_media.caption: Philosophical questions become clearer when rival answers give reasons and face the same case. Different lenses can expose consequences, duties and relationships without automatically settling the answer.

nodes.title: Learning How to Learn
nodes.goal: Attention, note-taking, spacing and recall.

quiz.prompt: Leo has a test in one week on 20 vocabulary words. Which plan uses spaced repetition, the study method proven to help memory most?
quiz.answer: Review the words a little each day all week, testing himself from memory.
quiz.explain: Spaced repetition means reviewing material in short sessions spread over days, which builds stronger, longer-lasting memory than cramming.
choices: Wait until he happens to feel like studying, which may well never happen.
Copy the whole list out neatly one single time and then never look at it again.
Read the words over and over for three straight hours the night before the test.
Review the words a little each day all week, testing himself from memory.

quiz.prompt: While studying, Nina stops and asks herself, 'Do I actually understand this part, or am I just recognizing the words?' This habit of watching and checking your own thinking is called what?
quiz.answer: Metacognition
quiz.explain: Metacognition is thinking about your own thinking, such as checking whether you truly understand something.
choices: Photosynthesis
Handwriting
Metacognition
Multiplication

quiz.prompt: Leo studies for 15 minutes a day on each of 6 days instead of doing one long session. How many minutes of study is that altogether?
quiz.explain: 15 minutes on each of 6 days gives 15 x 6 = 90 minutes, spread out so memory has time to consolidate.

quiz.prompt: Ana and Bo prepare for the same test. Ana re-reads the chapter four times. Bo closes the book, writes down what he can remember, then checks what he missed. What does research on learning predict?
quiz.answer: Bo will remember more
choices: Ana will remember more, since she saw the words more often.
Both of them will remember about the same amount.
Neither method has any effect on memory.
Bo will remember more
quiz.explain: Because pulling facts out of memory strengthens them more than re-reading does. Retrieval practice, testing yourself and checking, builds far stronger memories than re-reading, which feels easy but leaves little behind.

quiz.prompt: Halfway down a page, Sena notices she has read three pages without taking in a single word. What is the most useful thing for her to do next?
quiz.answer: Go back and read those pages actively.
choices: Keep reading forwards and hope the meaning comes back to her later.
Start the whole book again at page one, reading it very slowly.
Go back and read those pages actively.
Highlight the three pages in bright yellow and then carry on quickly.
quiz.explain: Noticing the lapse is the useful part; the fix is to reread with a question in mind so the words are actually processed.

quiz.prompt: Jae says, 'I highlighted the whole page, so I know it.' Why is highlighting a weak test of whether you understand something?
quiz.answer: Marking text does not require pulling ideas out of memory.
choices: Bright colors make text harder to read.
Marking text does not require pulling ideas out of memory.
A highlighted page looks impressive to a teacher marking the work.
Highlighting a page takes longer than reading it carefully once.
quiz.explain: Highlighting can be done while barely thinking. A real check asks you to recall or explain the idea without looking.

quiz.prompt: Tomas re-reads his notes, everything feels familiar, so he stops studying. He then does poorly on the test. What went wrong?
quiz.answer: Familiarity felt like knowing, but he never tested himself
choices: Familiarity felt like knowing, but he never tested himself
He read through the notes too slowly
His notes were far too short
He should have studied in a different room
quiz.explain: Recognising material is much easier than producing it. The test asks you to produce it, so your practice should too.

quiz.prompt: Mia reviews new words 1, 3, 7 and 14 days after learning them. If she learns them on 1 March, on which day of March is her last review?
quiz.explain: 14 days after 1 March is 15 March. Reviews that get further apart each time are the core of spaced repetition.

quiz.prompt: Two students revise the same chapter. One writes questions and answers them from memory; the other copies the chapter neatly into a new notebook. Which prediction does research on learning best support?
quiz.answer: The first student will remember more
choices: The first student will remember more
The second will, because writing things out helps
Both will do the same, since both spent equal time
Neither method makes any difference to memory
quiz.explain: Copying keeps the material in front of you; retrieving it makes your brain do the work, and that effort is what builds the memory.

quiz.prompt: You have four subjects to revise and one week. Explain why one subject a day beats cramming all four into a single long session on the last day, using two ideas about memory.
quiz.answer: Spacing the practice across days lets a little forgetting happen between sessions, and each return then demands effortful retrieval, which strengthens memory far more than one long massed session that feels easy at the time and fades quickly.
quiz.explain: Spacing and retrieval practice are the two best-supported study findings in psychology, and they work against how studying feels.

lesson_media.alt: Two recall-strength curves compare a single cram session that fades steeply with four spaced retrieval sessions that repeatedly boost recall and decay more slowly across days.
lesson_media.caption: Spacing allows some forgetting before retrieval, making practice effortful and durable. The exact curve varies, but repeated recall generally outperforms one massed review.

nodes.title: Formal Logic
nodes.goal: Propositional and predicate logic; arguments and proofs.

lesson_media.alt: A four-row brass switchboard shows every setting of two switches; three result lamps glow, while only the row with the first switch on and the second switch off has an unlit lamp.
lesson_media.caption: A material implication is false only when its first proposition is true and its second proposition is false.

lesson_media.title: Build a truth table
lesson_media.instructions: Toggle the two propositions and compare AND, OR and IMPLIES. Watch the complete four-row table update and find the single false implication case.

quiz.prompt: Consider the argument: 'If it rains, the picnic is cancelled. The picnic was not cancelled. Therefore, it did not rain.' Which describes this argument?
quiz.answer: Valid, by modus tollens: denying the consequent denies the antecedent.
quiz.explain: From 'if P then Q' and 'not Q', modus tollens validly concludes 'not P'.
choices: Invalid, because it commits the fallacy of denying the antecedent.
Invalid, because it commits the fallacy of affirming the consequent.
Valid, because any argument about rain and picnics is automatically sound.
Valid, by modus tollens: denying the consequent denies the antecedent.

quiz.prompt: Let the domain be all people. Let L(x) mean 'x likes music.' Which predicate-logic formula correctly says 'Not everyone likes music'?
quiz.answer: ¬∀x L(x)
quiz.explain: 'Not everyone likes music' negates the universal claim, which is ¬∀x L(x), equivalent to ∃x ¬L(x); ∀x ¬L(x) wrongly says nobody likes music.
choices: ∀x ¬L(x)
∃x L(x)
¬∀x L(x)
¬∃x L(x)

quiz.prompt: A propositional formula is built from 3 distinct atomic variables (P, Q, R). How many rows does its complete truth table have?
quiz.explain: Each variable can be true or false independently, so a table for n variables has 2^n rows; 2^3 = 8.

quiz.prompt: A student writes: 'If a number is divisible by 4, it is even. 12 is even. Therefore 12 is divisible by 4.' The conclusion happens to be true. What is the verdict on the argument?
quiz.answer: Invalid: it affirms the consequent.
choices: Valid, because the conclusion turns out to be true in this particular case.
Valid, because 12 really is divisible by four without leaving a remainder.
Invalid: it affirms the consequent.
Invalid, because the premise about divisibility and evenness is false.
quiz.explain: Validity concerns form, not the luck of a true conclusion. From 'if P then Q' and Q, nothing follows about P.

quiz.prompt: Which formula is logically equivalent to ¬(P ∧ Q)?
quiz.answer: ¬P ∨ ¬Q, by De Morgan's law
choices: ¬P ∧ ¬Q
P ∨ Q
¬P → Q
¬P ∨ ¬Q, by De Morgan's law
quiz.explain: De Morgan's law turns the negation of a conjunction into a disjunction of negations: it fails that both hold exactly when at least one fails.

quiz.prompt: An argument is valid, but its conclusion is false. What else must be true of it?
quiz.answer: At least one premise is false.
choices: The argument is sound.
At least one premise is false.
The argument contains a formal fallacy somewhere.
The conclusion is unrelated to the premises.
quiz.explain: A valid argument transmits truth from premises to conclusion, so a false conclusion means some premise must be false.

quiz.prompt: Consider: 'Every student who passed studied. Ada studied.' What follows about Ada?
quiz.answer: Nothing follows about whether Ada passed
choices: Nothing follows about whether Ada passed
Ada passed the course
Ada did not pass the course
Some student who studied also passed
quiz.explain: Studying is necessary for passing here, not sufficient. Treating a necessary condition as sufficient is the fallacy of affirming the consequent.

quiz.prompt: In the truth table for P → Q, how many of the four rows make the formula false?
quiz.explain: A conditional is false only when the antecedent is true and the consequent false, which happens in exactly one of the four rows.

quiz.prompt: A student claims that from ¬(P ∨ Q) one may infer ¬P. Which verdict is correct?
quiz.answer: Correct, since ¬(P ∨ Q) is equivalent to ¬P ∧ ¬Q
choices: Correct, since ¬(P ∨ Q) is equivalent to ¬P ∧ ¬Q
Incorrect, because the negation applies to the disjunction as a whole
Correct, though the same inference fails for ¬Q
Incorrect, since P might still turn out true
quiz.explain: One of De Morgan's laws: denying a disjunction denies both disjuncts. The symmetric inference to ¬Q is equally valid.

quiz.prompt: Explain the difference between an argument being valid and its conclusion being true, and give one valid argument with a false conclusion.
quiz.answer: Validity concerns form: if the premises were true, the conclusion would have to be true. So an argument can be valid with a false premise and therefore a false conclusion, for example 'All birds are mammals; a robin is a bird; so a robin is a mammal.'
quiz.explain: Soundness is validity plus true premises. Keeping the two apart is what lets logic evaluate reasoning independently of the facts.

nodes.title: Critical Thinking
nodes.goal: Evidence, bias and reasoning under uncertainty.

quiz.prompt: A gambler notices a coin has landed heads five times in a row and bets heavily on tails next, insisting tails is 'due.' Assuming a fair coin, which cognitive bias is he showing?
quiz.answer: The gambler's fallacy: treating independent events as if connected.
quiz.explain: Each fair coin flip is independent, so the probability of tails stays 1/2 regardless of previous flips.
choices: The gambler's fallacy: treating independent events as if connected.
The halo effect: letting one good trait color his whole judgment.
The anchoring effect: relying too heavily on the first number he saw.
Confirmation bias: seeking only the evidence that supports his belief.

quiz.prompt: A wellness blog claims a tea cures colds. To evaluate this claim most rigorously using the scientific method, which piece of evidence should you weigh most heavily?
quiz.answer: A randomized controlled trial comparing tea-drinkers with a placebo group.
quiz.explain: A controlled trial with a comparison group isolates the tea's effect and guards against placebo and coincidence, unlike testimonials which cannot rule out natural recovery.
choices: The fact that this tea has been sold in shops for a great many years.
A randomized controlled trial comparing tea-drinkers with a placebo group.
The blogger's confident tone and the beautiful photographs of the tea.
Dozens of glowing testimonials from people who drank the tea and felt better.

quiz.prompt: Dana believes a certain diet works, so she reads only success stories and ignores studies showing it fails. Then she says, 'See, all the evidence I found supports it.' What is the flaw?
quiz.answer: Confirmation bias: she counted only the evidence that fit her belief.
quiz.explain: Selectively gathering only supportive evidence while ignoring contrary data is confirmation bias, which makes her conclusion unreliable.
choices: A valid conclusion, since she gathered a great deal of evidence.
A straw-man argument: she distorted her opponents' actual view.
Confirmation bias: she counted only the evidence that fit her belief.
The sunk-cost fallacy: she continued because she had invested effort.

quiz.prompt: Out of 10,000 people screened, 100 truly have a disease and the test detects all 100. Of the 9,900 who do not have it, 3% also test positive. How many people test positive in total?
quiz.explain: 100 true positives plus 3% of 9,900 (297) false positives gives 397 positives, so most positives are false alarms.

quiz.prompt: A radio show invites listeners to call in about a proposed law. 80% of callers oppose it, and the host announces that the country opposes the law. Which flaw matters most?
quiz.answer: The callers are a self-selected sample.
choices: Eighty percent is too slim a majority to draw any firm conclusion from.
Radio listeners tend to be less well informed than newspaper readers are.
The callers are a self-selected sample.
The law has not been in force long enough for anyone to judge it yet.
quiz.explain: People who bother to phone in are those with strong views, so the sample does not represent the wider population.

quiz.prompt: A study reports that students who eat breakfast get better grades, and a newspaper runs the headline 'Breakfast raises grades.' Which alternative explanation should worry you most?
quiz.answer: Households with steadier routines and more resources may produce both the breakfast and the grades.
choices: Breakfast cereals contain sugar, which is unhealthy.
Grades are recorded by teachers, not by scientists.
The study surveyed students rather than their parents.
Households with steadier routines and more resources may produce both the breakfast and the grades.
quiz.explain: A common cause can generate the association without breakfast doing anything, which is why an observed link cannot settle causation.

quiz.prompt: A test detects 90% of true cases. In a group of 5,000 people, 200 genuinely have the condition. How many of those 200 does the test detect?
quiz.explain: 90% of 200 is 180, so 20 true cases are missed. Sensitivity is only half the story; the false-positive rate matters too.

quiz.prompt: A newspaper reports that a town's cancer rate runs at triple the national average. The town has 900 residents and three cases were diagnosed last year. Which caution matters most?
quiz.answer: Small populations produce large rate swings by chance
choices: Small populations produce large rate swings by chance
Cancer rates cannot be compared between towns
Three cases is too few to diagnose accurately
The national average changes from year to year
quiz.explain: With small denominators, one or two extra cases moves the rate enormously. Extreme rates cluster in small places for purely statistical reasons.

quiz.prompt: A trial of a tutoring programme lets schools volunteer to take part, and the volunteers improve more than the rest. Which flaw does that design most clearly have?
quiz.answer: Schools that volunteer may differ from those that do not
choices: Schools that volunteer may differ from those that do not
The sample size was probably too small to detect a real effect
Improvement was measured using tests written by the tutors themselves
Tutoring effects take longer than a single school year to appear
quiz.explain: Self-selection means the comparison groups differ before the programme starts, so the outcome gap mixes the programme with whatever made them volunteer.

quiz.prompt: A friend says: 'I have never met anyone harmed by that policy, so it harms nobody.' Name the reasoning error and describe the evidence that would actually settle the question.
quiz.answer: This generalises from an unrepresentative anecdotal sample: the people he meets are not a random draw, and those most harmed may be least likely to be among them, so settling it requires population-level data comparing outcomes for those affected and those not.
quiz.explain: Personal experience is a biased sample of the world in ways that are usually invisible to the person sampling it.

lesson_media.alt: A five-step reasoning chain starts with a claim that a supplement improves sleep, turns it into a measurable prediction, compares a randomized group with a control, checks attrition and expectancy bias, and updates the claim with an effect size and uncertainty.
lesson_media.caption: Critical thinking asks what evidence a claim predicts, what alternative processes could mimic it, and how much the result should change confidence.

nodes.title: Psychology
nodes.goal: Cognition, development and behavior.

quiz.prompt: A four-year-old watches water poured from a short, wide glass into a tall, thin glass and now insists the tall glass has 'more' water, though nothing was added. According to Piaget, this shows the child has not yet mastered what?
quiz.answer: Conservation: quantity stays the same despite changes in shape.
quiz.explain: Conservation is the developmental understanding that amount is unchanged by rearrangement, which young preoperational children typically lack.
choices: Reinforcement: repeating a behavior that has been rewarded.
Object permanence: knowing objects still exist when out of sight.
Attachment: forming a strong emotional bond with a main caregiver.
Conservation: quantity stays the same despite changes in shape.

quiz.prompt: A student can remember a 7-digit phone number just long enough to dial it, but forgets it moments later. Which memory system is she relying on?
quiz.answer: Short-term (working) memory, which holds limited information briefly.
quiz.explain: Holding a few items for seconds while using them, then losing them, is the signature of limited-capacity short-term/working memory.
choices: Sensory memory, which persists only for a small fraction of a second.
Procedural memory, which stores motor skills like riding a bike.
Long-term memory, which stores information for years or decades.
Short-term (working) memory, which holds limited information briefly.

quiz.prompt: A dog owner rings a bell every time before feeding. Soon the dog salivates at the bell alone, before any food appears. In classical conditioning terms, what is the bell after this learning?
quiz.answer: A conditioned stimulus that now triggers a conditioned response.
quiz.explain: After being paired with food, the once-neutral bell becomes a conditioned stimulus that elicits the conditioned response of salivation.
choices: A negative reinforcer that removes an unpleasant hunger sensation.
A conditioned stimulus that now triggers a conditioned response.
An unconditioned stimulus that naturally causes salivation on its own.
A neutral stimulus that by itself still produces no response.

quiz.prompt: In a study with 200 participants, 30% correctly recalled the whole word list after one week. How many participants is that?
quiz.explain: 30% of 200 is 0.30 x 200 = 60 participants.

quiz.prompt: A child screams in a shop and the parent buys sweets to quiet him. Over the following weeks the screaming happens more often. Which explains this best?
quiz.answer: The tantrum was reinforced by the sweets.
choices: The child has developed a lasting fear of shops and of sweets.
Tantrums are inherited traits, so a parent's response is irrelevant.
The tantrum was reinforced by the sweets.
The parent's memory of the incident faded faster than the child's did.
quiz.explain: A behavior followed by a reward becomes more frequent. The sweets acted as positive reinforcement for screaming.

quiz.prompt: In Asch's line-judging studies, many participants gave an obviously wrong answer after hearing several other people give it first. What does this most directly demonstrate?
quiz.answer: Conformity to a unanimous group.
choices: Poor eyesight among participants.
Conformity to a unanimous group.
Loss of memory for the lines just presented.
A conditioned reflex learned during the experiment.
quiz.explain: Participants could see the correct answer perfectly well; social pressure from a unanimous majority moved their public responses.

quiz.prompt: A researcher gives one group a sugar pill described as a painkiller, and their reported pain drops. Which conclusion is best supported?
quiz.answer: Expectation can change reported experience
choices: Expectation can change reported experience
Sugar has a mild pain-relieving effect
The participants were lying about their pain
Pain reports are useless as measurements
quiz.explain: The placebo effect is why drug trials need a control group given an indistinguishable dummy treatment.

quiz.prompt: In a study, 45 of 150 participants conformed to a wrong majority answer. What percentage conformed?
quiz.explain: 45 divided by 150 is 0.30. Conformity rates in this range are typical of line-judgement studies, and they rise sharply with group size up to about three.

quiz.prompt: A teenager takes far bigger risks in a driving simulator when friends are watching than when alone. Which developmental account fits that finding best?
quiz.answer: Reward sensitivity matures earlier than impulse control
choices: Reward sensitivity matures earlier than impulse control
Teenagers misunderstand the rules of the simulator
Driving skill drops whenever someone is observing
Risk-taking is learned entirely from friends
quiz.explain: The dual-systems account holds that reward-seeking circuitry develops ahead of the prefrontal control that restrains it, and peer presence amplifies the reward side.

quiz.prompt: A parent stops a child's tantrum by giving in, and afterwards both the tantrums and the giving-in become more frequent. Explain both changes using reinforcement.
quiz.answer: The child's tantrum is positively reinforced by getting the sweet, so it increases; the parent's giving in is negatively reinforced by the tantrum stopping, so that behaviour increases too, and each side's behaviour keeps reinforcing the other.
quiz.explain: This mutual reinforcement trap is well documented in family research, and it explains why the pattern is so hard to break from inside.

lesson_media.alt: A reciprocal network places one child's classroom behavior at the center and connects neural and bodily state, cognition and emotion, family and peer context, and development over time, warning against a single-cause label.
lesson_media.caption: Psychological explanation spans biological, cognitive, social and developmental levels. Causes interact, and the same behavior can arise through different pathways.

nodes.title: Ethics
nodes.goal: How should we act? Major moral theories.

quiz.prompt: A doctor could secretly harvest one healthy patient's organs to save five dying patients. A strict act-utilitarian focused only on total lives saved might approve, yet most people recoil. Which objection best captures the standard deontological reason to refuse?
quiz.answer: It treats the patient merely as a means, violating the duty not to kill.
quiz.explain: Deontology judges acts by duties and rights, so killing an innocent person as a mere means is forbidden regardless of good consequences.
choices: The doctor might get caught, which would lower overall happiness.
It treats the patient merely as a means, violating the duty not to kill.
The five patients never consented to receiving another person's organs.
Saving five lives does not really produce more happiness than saving one.

quiz.prompt: Aisha helps an elderly neighbor not because a rule commands it or because she calculated the happiness produced, but because she is becoming a compassionate, generous person and that is what such a person does. Which ethical theory best describes her reasoning?
quiz.answer: Virtue ethics, which focuses on character and being a good person.
quiz.explain: Virtue ethics centers on cultivating good character traits and acting as a virtuous person would, rather than on rules or consequences.
choices: Virtue ethics, which focuses on character and being a good person.
Utilitarianism, which focuses on maximizing overall well-being.
Deontology, which focuses on following moral duties and rules.
Ethical egoism, which focuses on advancing one's own self-interest.

quiz.prompt: A town can build a factory that raises total wealth and happiness for the majority but pollutes a small neighborhood, harming a few families badly. A utilitarian and a rights-based deontologist are most likely to disagree about which question?
quiz.answer: Whether the gain to the many can justify serious harm done to a few.
quiz.explain: Utilitarianism weighs total welfare and may accept the trade-off, while deontology insists individuals' rights cannot simply be outweighed by aggregate benefit.
choices: Whether the factory pollution is physically bad for human lungs.
Whether most of the townspeople would enjoy having the new jobs.
Whether the new factory will actually manage to make any real money.
Whether the gain to the many can justify serious harm done to a few.

quiz.prompt: A friend asks you to tell a small lie to spare her mild embarrassment. Explain how a utilitarian and a deontologist could reach different verdicts.
quiz.answer: A utilitarian weighs the consequences and may permit the lie if it reduces harm overall, while a deontologist holds that lying breaks a duty of truthfulness and is wrong whatever the outcome.
quiz.explain: The two theories differ in what they look at: utilitarianism looks forward to results, deontology looks at the kind of act being performed.

quiz.prompt: A company argues that a practice must be acceptable because it has always been done that way in the industry. Which reply best identifies the mistake?
quiz.answer: What is customary need not be right.
choices: Industries change their practices far too slowly to be trusted on this.
The company ought to hold a vote among all of its own employees first.
What is customary need not be right.
Customs are older than laws, so the law should be followed instead.
quiz.explain: Appealing to tradition describes what people do, which by itself cannot establish what they ought to do.

quiz.prompt: A city can fund a bus route that saves many commuters a few minutes, or one that transforms life for a small isolated village. Which consideration is distinctively one of justice rather than of total benefit?
quiz.answer: Whether the villagers are owed access that the majority already enjoys.
choices: Which route produces the larger total saving in travel time.
Which route more of the city's residents would vote for.
Which route costs the city less to run each year.
Whether the villagers are owed access that the majority already enjoys.
quiz.explain: Questions of justice ask about entitlements and fair shares, which can pull against simply maximizing the aggregate benefit.

quiz.prompt: A shopkeeper is honest with customers because dishonesty would cost him business. A philosopher says the action is right but tells us nothing about his character. Which framework does that judgement come from?
quiz.answer: Virtue ethics
choices: Virtue ethics
Utilitarianism, which weighs the shopkeeper's profit alone
Deontology
Relativism, which denies that honesty has value
quiz.explain: Which asks what an act shows about the person. Virtue ethics evaluates the agent's settled dispositions, so it can call an act right while withholding praise from the motive behind it.

quiz.prompt: A hospital must choose between a treatment that saves 10 lives with certainty and one with a 50% chance of saving 30. Which consideration does a utilitarian weigh most heavily?
quiz.answer: The expected number of lives saved
choices: The expected number of lives saved
Whether the doctors intended each death
Whether the patients consented to the risk
Which treatment costs the hospital less
quiz.explain: Expected value is 10 against 15, so the utilitarian leans to the gamble. Intention and consent are the considerations other frameworks put first.

quiz.prompt: A charity has $9,000. Programme A saves one life per $1,500 and programme B saves one life per $900. If it spends the whole budget on the more efficient programme, how many lives does it save?
quiz.explain: 9,000 divided by 900 is 10, against 6 for programme A. Cost-effectiveness reasoning of this kind is central to effective altruism and controversial for the same reason.

quiz.prompt: A promise made in private is broken, nobody ever finds out, and nobody is harmed. Explain why a consequentialist and a deontologist reach different verdicts, and state what each treats as decisive.
quiz.answer: The consequentialist treats outcomes as decisive, so with no harm there is little or nothing wrong; the deontologist treats the duty created by the promise as decisive whatever the consequences, since on that view the wrong lies in the act of breaking it and in the intention behind it.
quiz.explain: Cases with no bad consequences are designed to isolate exactly where the two theories locate wrongness.

lesson_media.alt: Three columns evaluate whether to break a promise to prevent serious harm: consequentialism compares outcomes, deontology tests duties and universalizable rules, and virtue or care ethics examines character, relationships and vulnerability.
lesson_media.caption: Moral theories organize reasons differently. Applying each to the same hard case reveals both its insight and the questions it leaves unresolved.

nodes.title: History of Philosophy
nodes.goal: From Socrates to the moderns.

quiz.prompt: Socrates was known for a distinctive method of teaching and inquiry. Which best describes the 'Socratic method'?
quiz.answer: Asking probing questions to expose contradictions and refine ideas.
quiz.explain: The Socratic method uses persistent questioning to reveal assumptions and contradictions, drawing understanding out of the interlocutor rather than lecturing.
choices: Asking probing questions to expose contradictions and refine ideas.
Conducting careful laboratory experiments to test hypotheses.
Delivering long lectures that students memorized word for word.
Writing long, detailed textbooks that summarize all the known facts.

quiz.prompt: Plato's Theory of Forms holds that a perfect circle drawn on paper is only an imperfect copy of something. Of what?
quiz.answer: The eternal, non-physical Form of the Circle, imperfectly copied.
quiz.explain: For Plato, physical objects are imperfect participations in perfect, abstract Forms that exist independently of the material world.
choices: The atoms that make up the ink, which are the only real things.
A circle stored in the person's own short-term visual memory.
A better circle drawn by a more skilled artist somewhere on Earth.
The eternal, non-physical Form of the Circle, imperfectly copied.

quiz.prompt: Kant argued that we should act only on a principle we could will to become a universal law binding on everyone. What is this principle called?
quiz.answer: The categorical imperative.
quiz.explain: Kant's categorical imperative commands acting only on maxims one could consistently will to be universal laws, independent of desired outcomes.
choices: The social contract.
The greatest happiness principle.
The theory of recollection.
The categorical imperative.

quiz.prompt: Descartes tried to doubt everything he could, yet concluded 'I think, therefore I am.' Explain why he held that this one belief survived his doubt.
quiz.answer: Even doubting is a form of thinking, and thinking requires a thinker, so the very act of doubting shows that he exists.
quiz.explain: The attempt to doubt one's own existence defeats itself, since something must be doing the doubting.

quiz.prompt: Aristotle disagreed with his teacher Plato about where the essential nature of a thing is located. What was Aristotle's view?
quiz.answer: Forms exist in the things themselves.
choices: Forms exist in a separate eternal realm beyond the physical world.
Nothing has any nature at all, since everything is always changing.
Forms exist in the things themselves.
Only mathematical objects have natures; living things do not have any.
quiz.explain: Aristotle relocated form into the concrete substance, so the nature of a horse is found in horses rather than in a separate realm.

quiz.prompt: Hume pointed out that no matter how many sunrises we have observed, nothing guarantees the next one. Which problem was he raising?
quiz.answer: The problem of induction.
choices: The mind-body problem.
The problem of induction.
The problem of universals in metaphysics.
The problem of evil raised against theism.
quiz.explain: Induction moves from observed cases to unobserved ones, and Hume argued that no non-circular reasoning licenses that move.

quiz.prompt: A student says Socrates taught by telling his pupils the answers. Which feature of the dialogues most directly contradicts that?
quiz.answer: Socrates asks questions and often reaches no answer
choices: Socrates asks questions and often reaches no answer
Socrates wrote long treatises for his pupils to read
Socrates charged high fees for his lessons
Socrates taught mainly through written correspondence
quiz.explain: Many early dialogues end in aporia, with the question unresolved. Socrates wrote nothing; we have him through Plato and Xenophon.

quiz.prompt: Locke held that the mind starts as a blank sheet; Leibniz replied that the mind brings something of its own. Which observation would count in Leibniz's favour?
quiz.answer: Children acquire grammar faster than the speech they hear explains
choices: Children acquire grammar faster than the speech they hear explains
Children copy the accent of the people around them
Adults forget almost all of their early childhood
Some children learn to read earlier than others
quiz.explain: The poverty-of-the-stimulus argument, revived by Chomsky, is the modern descendant of Leibniz's reply to Locke.

quiz.prompt: Socrates was executed in 399 BC and Aristotle died in 322 BC. How many years separate the two events?
quiz.explain: 399 - 322 = 77 years, which covers the whole span from Socrates through Plato's Academy to Aristotle's own school.

quiz.prompt: Hume argued that we never observe causation itself, only one event following another. Explain his argument and one reason philosophers have resisted the conclusion.
quiz.answer: We observe constant conjunction and succession but never a necessary connection between the events, so Hume concludes the idea of cause comes from habit rather than from reason or observation; philosophers resist because science treats causal claims as supporting interventions and counterfactuals, and mere habit looks too weak to justify that.
quiz.explain: Hume's problem still shapes work on causation, from probabilistic accounts to interventionist theories.

lesson_media.alt: A timeline links Socratic questioning in fifth-century BCE Athens, Plato and Aristotle, Hellenistic schools, medieval philosophy in Arabic, Hebrew and Latin traditions, and early modern debates on knowledge and politics, emphasizing transmission and dispute.
lesson_media.caption: Philosophical history is a network of arguments, translations and institutions. A Socrates-to-moderns route is one path through a much larger global history.

nodes.title: Social Sciences
nodes.goal: Sociology, anthropology and how we study societies.

quiz.prompt: A researcher spends a year living in a remote village, participating in daily life and taking detailed field notes to understand its kinship customs from the inside. This method, central to cultural anthropology, is called what?
quiz.answer: Ethnography: participant observation.
quiz.explain: Ethnography involves immersive, long-term participant observation to understand a culture from within, a hallmark of anthropology.
choices: A double-blinded clinical drug trial.
A nationwide written census survey.
Ethnography: participant observation.
A controlled laboratory experiment.
