quiz.prompt: A sociologist finds that towns with more coffee shops also have higher average incomes, and concludes coffee shops make people rich. What is the main flaw in this reasoning?
quiz.answer: Correlation does not imply causation; a third factor may cause both.
quiz.explain: A statistical association between two variables can arise from a common cause, so correlation alone cannot establish that one causes the other.
choices: Sociologists are not permitted to study businesses like coffee shops.
Income figures collected from small towns are never reliable enough.
Correlation does not imply causation; a third factor may cause both.
The two things obviously cannot be related to each other at all.

quiz.prompt: To measure public support for a new policy across a whole country cheaply and quickly, which social-science method is most appropriate?
quiz.answer: A survey of a large, representative random sample.
quiz.explain: Surveys of representative random samples efficiently estimate the attitudes of a large population, which is their central strength.
choices: A survey of a large, representative random sample.
A close literary reading of one historical novel.
A year-long ethnography of one single household.
A laboratory chemistry experiment on soil samples.

quiz.prompt: A survey of 800 people finds that 45% support a new policy. How many respondents is that?
quiz.explain: 45% of 800 is 0.45 x 800 = 360 respondents.

quiz.prompt: A pollster asks, 'Do you support the sensible new safety law?' Support comes back extremely high. What is the main problem?
quiz.answer: The wording praises the law
choices: The sample was probably far too large.
Safety is popular anyway.
Polls should be run by governments.
The wording praises the law
quiz.explain: Which pushes respondents toward agreeing. A leading question builds the answer into the wording, so the result measures the phrasing as much as opinion.

quiz.prompt: Researchers want to know whether a job-training program raises earnings, and compare trainees with people who never applied. Why might this comparison mislead?
quiz.answer: People who apply may differ from those who do not.
choices: Earnings figures collected by government agencies are broadly unreliable.
Training programs lie outside the scope of social science.
People who apply may differ from those who do not.
The two groups would have to be measured in different currencies.
quiz.explain: Self-selection means applicants may already be more motivated or employable, so any earnings gap confounds the program with the people.

quiz.prompt: A survey of 1,200 people has a margin of error of about 3 percentage points. If 52% support a policy, what is the lower end of the range, in percent?
quiz.explain: 52 - 3 = 49, so the true figure may sit below half. Reporting a lead inside the margin of error as a result is one of the commonest polling errors.

quiz.prompt: A district assigns pupils to large and small classes at random to test whether class size raises scores. Why does randomisation matter here?
quiz.answer: It makes the groups comparable on things nobody measured
choices: It makes the groups comparable on things nobody measured
It increases the number of pupils in the study
It guarantees the result will be statistically significant
It removes measurement error from the tests
quiz.explain: Randomisation balances unobserved as well as observed differences in expectation, which is exactly what statistical controls cannot do.

quiz.prompt: An interviewer asks families about their income and a quarter refuse to answer, with poorer and richer households refusing at different rates. Which problem does that create?
quiz.answer: Non-response bias in the estimated average income
choices: Non-response bias in the estimated average income
A smaller sample and so a wider margin of error only
A coding error in the questionnaire design
A confound between income and household size
quiz.explain: If refusal correlates with the variable being measured, the shortfall shifts the estimate rather than merely widening its interval.

quiz.prompt: A study finds that people who attend religious services live longer, controlling for income and education. Explain why a sociologist would still hesitate to call attendance the cause.
quiz.answer: Controls handle only the variables actually measured: healthier people may simply be more able to attend, which is reverse causation through selection, and unmeasured confounders such as social support or baseline health could produce the association without attendance causing anything.
quiz.explain: Adding controls narrows but never closes the gap between association and causation in observational data.

lesson_media.alt: A five-step social research process moves from a question about why park use differs by neighborhood through operational definitions and sampling, surveys plus observation and interviews, pattern comparison, and limits and alternative explanations.
lesson_media.caption: Social science turns broad concepts into observable measures, samples people and settings, combines methods and states what its design cannot establish.

nodes.title: Epistemology
nodes.goal: Knowledge, justification and truth.

quiz.prompt: In a classic Gettier case, Smith justifiably believes 'the person who will get the job has ten coins in their pocket' based on strong but misleading evidence about Jones; in fact Smith himself gets the job and happens, unknown to him, to have ten coins. His belief is true and justified, yet we hesitate to call it knowledge. What does this challenge?
quiz.answer: The traditional analysis of knowledge as justified true belief.
quiz.explain: Gettier cases present justified true beliefs that intuitively fail to be knowledge, showing that justified-true-belief is insufficient.
choices: The distinction between a priori and a posteriori kinds of knowledge.
The claim that truth is objective and wholly independent of minds.
The idea that beliefs can ever be justified by evidence at all.
The traditional analysis of knowledge as justified true belief.

quiz.prompt: A foundationalist and a coherentist disagree about the structure of justification. Which claim is distinctively foundationalist?
quiz.answer: Some beliefs are basic and self-justifying, and all other justified beliefs rest on them.
quiz.explain: Foundationalism holds that justification terminates in basic beliefs that support the rest, unlike coherentism's mutually supporting web.
choices: No belief is ever justified, so knowledge is impossible.
Some beliefs are basic and self-justifying, and all other justified beliefs rest on them.
Justification depends entirely on the reliability of the belief-forming process.
A belief is justified only by how well it coheres with the whole web of one's other beliefs.

quiz.prompt: A skeptic argues you cannot know you have hands because you cannot rule out being a brain in a vat fed false experiences. Which response best captures a reliabilist reply?
quiz.answer: If your perceptual processes are reliable, your belief counts as knowledge.
quiz.explain: Reliabilism grounds knowledge in the actual reliability of belief-forming processes, so knowledge does not require refuting every skeptical hypothesis.
choices: You can introspect and simply feel certain that your hands are real.
If your perceptual processes are reliable, your belief counts as knowledge.
Since the belief coheres with your other beliefs, it is automatically true.
The skeptic must be wrong because skepticism is far too depressing.

quiz.prompt: A hiker glances at a station clock at exactly 3:00 and forms the true belief that it is 3:00. The clock stopped a day earlier. Explain why epistemologists deny that she knows the time.
quiz.answer: Her belief is true only by luck: the stopped clock is an unreliable source, so the process that produced the belief is disconnected from the fact that makes it true.
quiz.explain: Knowledge requires the right connection between belief and fact; here the connection is severed and the match is accidental.

quiz.prompt: Two jurors hear identical testimony. One already believed the defendant guilty and now feels certain; the other suspends judgment until forensic results arrive. Name the epistemic failing of the first juror:
quiz.answer: Treating evidence as confirming a belief already fixed.
choices: Failing to notice that testimony is weaker evidence than forensics.
Demanding a standard of certainty that no courtroom could ever supply.
Treating evidence as confirming a belief already fixed.
Confusing the reliability of a witness with the sincerity of a witness.
quiz.explain: When a prior belief determines how evidence is read, the evidence stops doing justificatory work and merely echoes the belief.

quiz.prompt: You believe your friend is in Paris because she sent you a photo of the Eiffel Tower. She is in Paris, but the photo was an old one she resent by mistake. Assess your belief:
quiz.answer: It is true and justified, but a Gettier-style accident sits between the evidence and the fact that makes it true.
choices: It is false, because the photograph was old.
It is unjustified, since photographs justify nothing.
It is knowledge in the full sense: the belief is true, she sincerely held it, and a photograph is about as good as evidence ever gets.
It is true and justified, but a Gettier-style accident sits between the evidence and the fact that makes it true.
quiz.explain: Justified true belief that is true by luck rather than in virtue of the justification is the standard shape of a Gettier case.

quiz.prompt: A weather service gets 95% of its forecasts right by design; today it predicts rain and rain falls. A colleague guesses rain on a hunch and also gets it right. Which epistemic difference matters most?
quiz.answer: One belief came from a reliable process
choices: One belief came from a reliable process
One believer felt more confident about it
One belief arrived earlier in the day
One believer had glanced at the sky
quiz.explain: Reliabilism locates the difference in the process rather than the outcome, which is why both can hold a true belief while only one counts as knowing.

quiz.prompt: Two scientists hold the same true theory. One can cite the experiments; the other believes it because a charismatic teacher said so. Which verdict fits the standard analysis of knowledge?
quiz.answer: The second lacks the justification that knowledge requires
choices: The second lacks the justification that knowledge requires
Both count as knowing, since the theory holds true
Neither counts, because theories change over time
The first lacks knowledge, having relied on others' experiments
quiz.explain: True belief without justification falls short on the traditional account; testimony can justify, but deference to charisma without any check on reliability does not.

quiz.prompt: A juror assigns prior probability 0.2 to guilt. A piece of evidence occurs with probability 0.8 if the defendant is guilty and 0.1 if innocent. Compute the posterior probability of guilt to two decimal places.
quiz.explain: Bayes: (0.2 x 0.8) = 0.16 against (0.8 x 0.1) = 0.08, so 0.16 / 0.24 = 0.667. Strong-sounding evidence moves a low prior less than intuition suggests.

quiz.prompt: A student argues that since any belief can be doubted, nobody knows anything. Set out why the inference fails, distinguishing two senses of 'possible to doubt'.
quiz.answer: It conflates the bare logical possibility of error with a live, grounded reason to doubt: on most accounts knowledge requires justification rather than certainty, so a fallible belief with strong grounds can still be knowledge, and only a doubt supported by some actual reason defeats it.
quiz.explain: The move from fallibility to scepticism is where most sceptical arguments either succeed or fail, and where fallibilist replies concentrate.

lesson_media.alt: Three overlapping circles for belief, truth and justification meet at a region marked knowledge with a question mark; a Gettier pressure-test card shows all three checks satisfied through luck while the reason-to-truth link remains defective.
lesson_media.caption: The traditional analysis of knowledge as justified true belief is a useful starting point. Gettier cases show why the quality of the connection between justification and truth also matters.

nodes.title: Metaphysics
nodes.goal: Being, causation, free will and the mind.

quiz.prompt: A hard determinist and a compatibilist both accept that every event, including human choices, is fully caused by prior events. On what do they disagree?
quiz.answer: Whether caused choices can still count as free and responsible.
quiz.explain: Compatibilists say freedom is compatible with determinism if one acts on one's own desires without coercion, while hard determinists deny free will altogether.
choices: Whether the future is already fixed in just the way the past is.
Whether the physical world obeys strict causal laws at all.
Whether caused choices can still count as free and responsible.
Whether human beings ever actually make any decisions at all.

quiz.prompt: Substance dualism and physicalism give competing answers to the mind-body problem. Which is a core commitment of substance dualism?
quiz.answer: The mind is a non-physical substance distinct from the brain.
quiz.explain: Substance dualism, associated with Descartes, holds that mind and body are two distinct kinds of substance, one non-physical.
choices: Only physical things exist, and minds are just patterns of matter.
Consciousness is merely an illusion produced by our language.
The mind is a non-physical substance distinct from the brain.
Mental states are simply identical to physical states of the brain.

quiz.prompt: The 'interaction problem' is the classic objection to substance dualism. What exactly does it press?
quiz.answer: How a non-physical mind could causally affect a physical body.
quiz.explain: If mind and body are wholly different substances, it is unclear how they could interact causally, which is the central difficulty for dualism.
choices: Whether other people really do have minds much like our own.
How memories are stored and retrieved across spans of time.
How a non-physical mind could causally affect a physical body.
Why brains happen to require quite so much energy in order to work.

quiz.prompt: A wooden ship has every plank replaced one at a time; the discarded planks are then reassembled into a second ship. State the metaphysical question this forces, and one principled answer.
quiz.answer: It asks which object is identical to the original ship over time; one principled answer is that identity follows spatiotemporal continuity, making the repaired ship the original and the reassembled one a reconstruction.
quiz.explain: Cases like this test criteria of persistence: continuity of matter and continuity of form pull in opposite directions and must be adjudicated.

quiz.prompt: A neuroscientist can predict which button a subject will press seconds before the subject reports deciding. Asked whether this refutes free will, give the reply most consistent with compatibilism:
quiz.answer: No, because freedom requires acting from one's own desires, not uncaused choice.
choices: Yes, because predicting a person's behavior shows that some outside force coerced them.
No, because brain activity recorded in a laboratory has no bearing on ordinary action.
Yes, because free will requires that decisions be entirely uncaused by anything prior.
No, because freedom requires acting from one's own desires, not uncaused choice.
quiz.explain: Compatibilism already grants that choices are caused; what matters is whether the causes run through the agent's own deliberation rather than coercion.

quiz.prompt: A vase shatters when struck. A philosopher denies that the striking caused the shattering, saying we observe only one event following another and never perceive a link. Identify the position:
quiz.answer: A Humean regularity view, on which causation amounts to constant conjunction rather than any perceived necessity.
choices: An occasionalist view, on which God alone causes each event directly and created objects themselves never cause anything at all.
A powers view on which objects have real causal capacities.
A determinist view on which every event has a full cause.
A Humean regularity view, on which causation amounts to constant conjunction rather than any perceived necessity.
quiz.explain: Hume's point was epistemic and then metaphysical: we see succession and regularity, not a necessary connection between the two events.

quiz.prompt: A club persists for 200 years though no founding member remains and its rules have all changed. One philosopher denies it remains the same club; another affirms it. Which question does the dispute turn on?
quiz.answer: What relation makes a thing at one time identical to one later
choices: What relation makes a thing at one time identical to one later
How long the club has kept the same name
Whether the members intended continuity
How many rules changed in each decade
quiz.explain: Diachronic identity asks which relation, if any, carries identity through change: material continuity, causal continuity, or something else.

quiz.prompt: A physicist claims the future stands fixed by the past plus the laws, and a colleague replies that this leaves deliberation pointless. Which compatibilist response addresses the reply best?
quiz.answer: Deliberation forms part of the causal chain that fixes the outcome
choices: Deliberation forms part of the causal chain that fixes the outcome
Quantum indeterminacy restores genuine openness
The laws hold only statistically at large scales
Nothing about human beings can be predicted anyway
quiz.explain: The compatibilist point is that determinism does not bypass deliberation; it runs through it, so deliberating remains the mechanism by which the outcome is determined.

quiz.prompt: In possible-worlds semantics a proposition holds necessarily when it holds at every world. Given exactly 4 worlds and a proposition true at 3 of them, how many worlds falsify its necessity?
quiz.explain: A single counterexample world is enough to defeat necessity, which is why necessity claims are so much stronger than truth claims.

quiz.prompt: A statue and the lump of clay it consists of occupy the same place at the same time, yet the lump survives being squashed and the statue does not. Set out the puzzle this creates and one philosophical response.
quiz.answer: By Leibniz's law identical things share all their properties, so a difference in what each can survive suggests statue and lump are not identical, yet they coincide materially and seem to be one object; one response is constitution, holding that the lump constitutes the statue without being identical to it, and another denies that the modal difference is genuine.
quiz.explain: The statue and the clay is the standard vehicle for material constitution and for arguments about modal properties.

lesson_media.alt: A common-cause model shows C pointing separately to A and B with no A-to-B arrow; a second panel presents, as one interventionist test, the qualified question of whether a well-defined do-A changes B under the stated model and background conditions.
lesson_media.caption: A common cause can make two events covary without either causing the other. Interventionism is one influential framework for probing causal dependence, not a complete or uncontested definition of metaphysical causation.

nodes.title: Cognitive Science
nodes.goal: Mind as computation across disciplines.

quiz.prompt: The 'computational theory of mind' is a foundational idea in cognitive science. Which statement best expresses it?
quiz.answer: Cognition is information processing over mental representations.
quiz.explain: The computational theory treats the mind as processing information by manipulating internal representations, allowing thought to be studied across disciplines.
choices: The brain is literally made out of silicon microchips and wires.
Thinking is impossible to study using any scientific method.
Only digital computers, and never brains, can really think.
Cognition is information processing over mental representations.

quiz.prompt: Cognitive science is often described as interdisciplinary. A researcher studies how neural firing patterns in the visual cortex give rise to the experience of recognizing a face. Which combination of fields is she most directly bridging?
quiz.answer: Neuroscience and psychology.
quiz.explain: Linking brain activity (neuroscience) to mental phenomena like recognition (psychology) is exactly the kind of bridge cognitive science builds.
choices: Astrophysics and literature.
Neuroscience and psychology.
Meteorology and demography.
Hydrology and jurisprudence.

quiz.prompt: A patient with damage to a specific brain region can no longer form new long-term memories but retains old ones and normal intelligence. Cognitive scientists use such 'dissociations' primarily to argue what?
quiz.answer: That memory is not one system but several separable components.
quiz.explain: Selective deficits (dissociations) show that one cognitive function can fail while another is intact, evidence that the mind has functionally distinct modules.
choices: That the brain plays no important role at all in storing memories.
That old memories must be stored somewhere outside the body entirely.
That memory is not one system but several separable components.
That intelligence and memory are really one and the same thing.

quiz.prompt: In a Stroop task, a participant averages 620 ms on congruent trials and 890 ms on incongruent trials. Report the interference effect in milliseconds.
quiz.explain: The Stroop interference effect is the incongruent minus congruent difference: 890 - 620 = 270 ms.

quiz.prompt: A model of reading predicts that recognition slows as words get rarer. In the data, rare words are recognized just as fast when they appear in a strongly predictive sentence. Choose the best interpretation:
quiz.answer: Top-down context contributes to recognition.
choices: Word frequency has no measurable influence on recognition speed anywhere.
Reading runs strictly bottom-up from letters to meaning.
Top-down context contributes to recognition.
The participants must have memorized the rare words before the session.
quiz.explain: Context supplying part of the work is the classic evidence that recognition is interactive rather than purely bottom-up.

quiz.prompt: A neural network trained on English verbs starts producing 'goed' before recovering 'went'. Critics had claimed this U-shaped pattern requires an explicit rule module. State what the network result shows:
quiz.answer: A system with no explicit rule can produce the pattern, so the pattern alone does not establish a rule module.
choices: Children do not in fact make errors of this kind.
Networks learn irregular verbs purely by memorizing whole words, so a network's output can tell us nothing about how children learn them.
Explicit rules are stored in the network's weights.
A system with no explicit rule can produce the pattern, so the pattern alone does not establish a rule module.
quiz.explain: The result removes the inference from behavior to architecture: overregularization is compatible with more than one underlying mechanism.

quiz.prompt: Participants recall a word list better when tested in the room where they learned it. Which account of memory does that finding support most directly?
quiz.answer: Retrieval depends on cues shared with encoding
choices: Retrieval depends on cues shared with encoding
Memories decay at a fixed rate over time
Rooms carry emotional associations that boost attention
Recall improves whenever participants feel relaxed
quiz.explain: Encoding specificity: what gets stored includes contextual cues, so overlap between study and test context aids retrieval.

quiz.prompt: A model of object recognition performs well on photographs but fails when the objects appear rotated. Which limitation does that failure most directly reveal?
quiz.answer: The learned representations depend on viewpoint
choices: The learned representations depend on viewpoint
The training set contained too few categories
The model lacks any language module
Rotation degrades the resolution of the image
quiz.explain: Viewpoint invariance is a specific computational achievement, and failure under rotation shows the model learned view-specific features instead.

quiz.prompt: A visual search task takes 400 ms with 4 items and 1,000 ms with 12 items. Assuming a linear serial search, compute the per-item slope in milliseconds.
quiz.explain: 600 ms extra across 8 extra items gives 75 ms per item. Slopes near zero indicate parallel search; steep slopes indicate item-by-item scanning.

quiz.prompt: A patient can name tools but not animals after a stroke. Explain what this dissociation suggests about semantic memory, and one reason a single case cannot settle the question.
quiz.answer: The category-specific deficit suggests semantic memory has some organisation by category, or by the sensory and functional features that distinguish living things from manufactured ones; a single case cannot settle it because one lesion may span several regions and the two categories differ in difficulty and familiarity, so a double dissociation across patients is needed.
quiz.explain: Double dissociations are the standard neuropsychological tool for arguing that two abilities depend on separable systems.

lesson_media.alt: A reciprocal network puts successful navigation at the center and connects computational goal, algorithmic representation, neural implementation and evidence from psychology, neuroscience, linguistics, philosophy and artificial intelligence.
lesson_media.caption: Cognitive science explains one capacity at multiple levels. A task description, information-processing strategy and physical implementation constrain one another without being interchangeable.

nodes.title: Moral Philosophy
nodes.goal: Metaethics and applied ethics in depth.

quiz.prompt: Metaethics asks second-order questions about the nature of morality rather than telling us what to do. Which of the following is a metaethical question?
quiz.answer: Are moral claims like 'stealing is wrong' objectively true or false?
quiz.explain: Metaethics studies the status and meaning of moral claims themselves, whereas the other options are first-order normative or applied questions.
choices: Are moral claims like 'stealing is wrong' objectively true or false?
Ought wealthy nations to accept far more refugees than they now do?
Should this hospital ration ventilators by age or by survival odds?
Is it permissible to eat meat given the suffering it causes animals?

quiz.prompt: A moral anti-realist called an emotivist and a moral realist disagree about the sentence 'Cruelty is wrong.' Which position does the emotivist hold?
quiz.answer: The sentence expresses disapproval rather than stating any fact.
quiz.explain: Emotivism, a non-cognitivist view, treats moral utterances as expressions of attitude rather than truth-apt factual claims.
choices: The sentence describes what most cultures happen to believe.
The sentence is true because a divine command has made it so.
The sentence expresses disapproval rather than stating any fact.
The sentence reports a mind-independent moral fact about cruelty.

quiz.prompt: Someone argues: 'Pleasure is desired by everyone, therefore pleasure is desirable, therefore pleasure is the good.' A metaethicist objects that this slides from what people do desire to what is worthy of desire. This objection points to which alleged error?
quiz.answer: The naturalistic fallacy: inferring value from descriptive facts.
quiz.explain: Moving from what is desired (a fact) to what is good or desirable (a value) is the classic is-ought gap, or naturalistic fallacy.
choices: Begging the question about whether pleasure really exists at all.
The genetic fallacy: judging a claim purely by where it came from.
The naturalistic fallacy: inferring value from descriptive facts.
A false dilemma between seeking pleasure and avoiding all pain.

quiz.prompt: A public-health official argues that because seat belts reduce deaths, wearing them ought to be legally required. Identify the hidden premise the argument needs.
quiz.answer: It needs a normative premise, such as that the state ought to compel actions that prevent serious harm; the empirical fact about deaths alone yields no ought.
quiz.explain: No purely descriptive set of premises entails a conclusion about what ought to be done; a bridging evaluative premise must be supplied.

quiz.prompt: A moral error theorist and a cultural relativist both deny that there are objective moral facts. Distinguish them by what each says about the sentence 'Torture is wrong':
quiz.answer: The error theorist calls it false; the relativist calls it true relative to a culture.
choices: The error theorist calls it meaningless, while the relativist calls it a report of a private feeling.
Both call it true, but disagree over whether anyone could ever come to know that it is true.
The error theorist treats it as a command, while the relativist treats it as a prediction.
The error theorist calls it false; the relativist calls it true relative to a culture.
quiz.explain: Error theory keeps moral sentences truth-apt but says they are systematically false; relativism keeps them true, indexed to a standard.

quiz.prompt: Diverting a trolley by a lever kills one and saves five; pushing a large stranger onto the track kills one and saves five. Most people accept the first and refuse the second. Say what this pattern pressures:
quiz.answer: Any theory that counts only outcomes, since the outcomes are matched.
choices: The claim that five lives outweigh one.
Any theory that counts only outcomes, since the outcomes are matched.
The claim that people are able to reason well about hypothetical cases.
The view that moral duties can differ between strangers and close friends.
quiz.explain: If outcomes are identical and verdicts differ, something other than outcomes, such as the doing/allowing or means/side-effect distinction, is doing the work.

quiz.prompt: A committee argues that a practice counts as moral because their society approves of it, and a critic replies that this makes moral reform incoherent. Which position does the critic attack?
quiz.answer: Cultural relativism about moral truth
choices: Cultural relativism about moral truth
Moral realism of a naturalist kind
Emotivism about moral language
Rule consequentialism
quiz.explain: If majority approval settles rightness, a reformer arguing against current practice is by definition mistaken, which most people take as a reductio of the view.

quiz.prompt: A drug company sets a price few patients in poor countries can pay, while the underlying research drew largely on public grants. Which framing sharpens the ethical question most?
quiz.answer: Whether the public investment creates a claim on access
choices: Whether the public investment creates a claim on access
Whether the company acted legally under patent law
Whether the drug works better than the alternatives
Whether shareholders approved the pricing decision
quiz.explain: The interesting question concerns the moral significance of the funding's origin, not compliance with existing law, which is what the other options ask about.

quiz.prompt: A policy saves 500 lives at a cost of $2.5 billion. Compute the cost per life saved, in millions of dollars.
quiz.explain: 2,500 million divided by 500 is 5 million per life. Such figures are used to compare policies, and their use is itself an ethical question.

quiz.prompt: Someone argues that because a behaviour occurs throughout nature, it must be morally acceptable. Name the fallacy, and explain why naming it does not by itself refute the conclusion.
quiz.answer: This commits the naturalistic fallacy, moving from a descriptive claim about what is to a normative claim about what ought to be; naming it shows only that this argument fails, not that the conclusion is false, since some independent argument might still support the same conclusion.
quiz.explain: Distinguishing a bad argument from a false conclusion is itself a discipline; the fallacy fallacy is the mirror-image error.

lesson_media.alt: A four-level arrow chain separates a metaethical question about what wrong means from a normative principle, an applied case about allocating scarce medicine and the resulting transparent institutional procedure.
lesson_media.caption: Metaethics, normative ethics and applied ethics ask different questions. Keeping the levels distinct prevents a claim about moral language from silently deciding a policy case.

nodes.title: Philosophy of Science
nodes.goal: What makes science work, and where it stops.

quiz.prompt: Popper proposed falsifiability as a criterion to demarcate science. On his view, which feature makes a theory scientific?
quiz.answer: It makes risky predictions that could be refuted by observation.
quiz.explain: For Popper, a theory is scientific if it forbids certain observations, making it testable and falsifiable, rather than compatible with everything.
choices: It makes risky predictions that could be refuted by observation.
It can explain any possible outcome very comfortably after the fact.
It is believed by a very large number of respected experts.
It has never once been contradicted by any observer anywhere.

quiz.prompt: An astrologer claims their theory explains every personality and event, and whenever a prediction fails they add a new adjustment so nothing could ever count against it. By Popper's criterion, why is this a problem?
quiz.answer: A theory that no possible observation can falsify is not scientific.
quiz.explain: Immunizing a theory against all possible refutation removes its falsifiability, which for Popper is what disqualifies it as science.
choices: The theory is too precise and makes far too many risky predictions.
The theory has been tested and clearly refuted, so it is scientific.
The theory uses too much mathematics, which real science forbids.
A theory that no possible observation can falsify is not scientific.

quiz.prompt: Kuhn's notion of a 'paradigm shift' differs sharply from Popper's steady falsification. Which scenario best exemplifies a Kuhnian paradigm shift?
quiz.answer: Accumulating anomalies trigger a revolution that replaces a whole framework.
quiz.explain: Kuhn described science as long periods of 'normal science' punctuated by revolutions in which an entire paradigm is replaced, not incremental falsification.
choices: Accumulating anomalies trigger a revolution that replaces a whole framework.
A single experiment cleanly refutes one hypothesis, which is quietly discarded.
A long-accepted theory is confirmed once more by a routine measurement.
Scientists gather more data within an accepted framework without changing it.

quiz.prompt: A lab runs 40 independent significance tests, using a 5% threshold, on null hypotheses that are all in fact true. State how many false positives it should expect on average.
quiz.explain: With a 5% error rate per test and all nulls true, the expected number of significant results is 0.05 x 40 = 2.

quiz.prompt: Two theories fit every observation gathered so far but diverge about cases beyond the data. A philosopher says this is not a temporary shortage of evidence but a structural feature. Name what she is pointing to:
quiz.answer: Underdetermination of theory by evidence
choices: Falsification, which eliminates one theory at a time.
Confirmation bias among the experimenters.
The replication crisis in the sciences.
Underdetermination of theory by evidence
quiz.explain: Since any body of data consistent with one theory can be consistent with rivals. Underdetermination says the evidence alone does not fix a unique theory, so non-evidential virtues are invoked to choose between rivals.

quiz.prompt: A prediction fails, so a researcher adds an auxiliary assumption that accounts for the failure and generates no new testable prediction. Duhem and Quine noted some such moves are legitimate. State what marks this one as illegitimate:
quiz.answer: It buys rescue without adding testable content.
choices: Auxiliary assumptions are forbidden in properly conducted scientific work.
A theory that fails a prediction once should be abandoned immediately.
It buys rescue without adding testable content.
The researcher should have gathered a larger sample before testing.
quiz.explain: Adjusting auxiliaries is normal science; what makes a move ad hoc is that it restores fit while forfeiting new empirical consequences.

quiz.prompt: A theory predicts a particle at a precise mass, the detector finds nothing there, and the researchers propose that the detector missed it and adjust the expected signal. Which methodological question deserves attention first?
quiz.answer: Whether the adjustment yields new testable predictions
choices: Whether the adjustment yields new testable predictions
Whether the original theory had been published first
Whether the detector cost more than its rivals
Whether other teams accept the same theory
quiz.explain: Auxiliary adjustments are legitimate when they are independently testable and ad hoc when they only absorb the failure.

quiz.prompt: Two labs run the same experiment; one finds an effect and one does not, and the second lab's sample outnumbers the first tenfold. Which conclusion follows most safely?
quiz.answer: The smaller study's estimate carries less weight
choices: The smaller study's estimate carries less weight
The effect exists but appears only in small samples
The replication failure indicates fraud in the first lab
The two results cannot both inform a single estimate
quiz.explain: Precision scales with sample size, so a pooled estimate weights the larger study more; disagreement between studies is expected rather than scandalous.

quiz.prompt: The prior odds of a hypothesis stand at 1:4 against. Evidence arrives with a likelihood ratio of 12 in its favour. State the posterior odds in favour, as a number to one.
quiz.explain: Posterior odds equal prior odds times the likelihood ratio: (1/4) x 12 = 3, so 3:1 in favour. Odds form makes Bayesian updating a single multiplication.

quiz.prompt: A researcher claims a theory of history counts as scientific because every event examined confirms it. Explain, using Popper, why the claim undercuts itself, and give one limit of Popper's criterion.
quiz.answer: For Popper a theory earns scientific status by prohibiting outcomes, so a theory confirmed by every event forbids nothing and is unfalsifiable, which makes the boast a confession; the limit is that theories are tested only alongside auxiliary assumptions, so the Duhem-Quine point means a failed prediction never falsifies a theory in isolation.
quiz.explain: Popper's criterion remains a good heuristic and a poor algorithm, for exactly the holist reason Duhem and Quine identified.

lesson_media.alt: A theory leads to a risky prediction and calibrated test, then a prediction-versus-data diamond visibly branches to provisional corroboration when results fit within uncertainty or to an anomaly when they do not; anomaly checks and revision loop back to a new discriminating test.
lesson_media.caption: Scientific theories gain content by risking observations. A failed prediction may implicate the theory, measurement or auxiliary assumptions, so revision must generate further tests rather than merely protect the claim.

nodes.title: Decision & Behavioral Science
nodes.goal: How people actually decide.

quiz.prompt: In an experiment, most people refuse to pay $5 to replace a lost concert ticket but happily buy a $5 ticket after losing a $5 bill, even though the net cost is identical. This inconsistency is best explained by which behavioral concept?
quiz.answer: Mental accounting: people file money into separate mental categories.
quiz.explain: Mental accounting leads people to treat the 'entertainment budget' as already spent when the ticket is lost, even though rational choice treats all dollars as interchangeable.
choices: Mental accounting: people file money into separate mental categories.
The availability heuristic: judging by what comes easily to mind.
Hyperbolic discounting: sharply overvaluing immediate rewards.
The endowment effect: valuing something more once you already own it.

quiz.prompt: Prospect theory predicts that people react differently to gains and losses. A manager will likely take a big risk to avoid a sure loss but plays it safe to lock in a sure gain of the same size. Which principle does this illustrate?
quiz.answer: Loss aversion: risk-seeking for losses, risk-averse for gains.
quiz.explain: Prospect theory's value function makes losses loom larger than gains, producing risk-seeking to avoid losses and risk-aversion to secure gains.
choices: Expected-utility maximization applied perfectly and consistently.
Loss aversion: risk-seeking for losses, risk-averse for gains.
Perfect rationality as assumed by classical economic theory.
The sunk-cost fallacy quietly driving all of the manager's choices.

quiz.prompt: A government wants more employees to save for retirement. Behavioral science suggests a low-cost 'nudge' that preserves free choice. Which policy fits best?
quiz.answer: Automatically enroll employees in the plan while letting them opt out.
quiz.explain: A default-enrollment nudge harnesses status-quo bias to raise participation while preserving freedom to opt out, the hallmark of libertarian paternalism.
choices: Legally require everyone to save a fixed percentage with no exceptions.
Do nothing and assume people will calculate the optimal savings rate.
Automatically enroll employees in the plan while letting them opt out.
Legally ban all household spending on non-essential consumer goods.

quiz.prompt: A lottery ticket costs $8 and pays $50 with probability 0.2 and nothing otherwise. Compute the expected monetary value of buying one ticket, in dollars.
quiz.explain: Expected payoff is 0.2 x 50 = 10 dollars; subtracting the 8 dollar price gives an expected value of 2 dollars.

quiz.prompt: When a coffee shop raises its price by 10%, the quantity it sells falls by 25%. Compute the price elasticity of demand, as a negative number.
quiz.explain: Elasticity is the percentage change in quantity divided by the percentage change in price: -25 / 10 = -2.5, so demand is elastic.

quiz.prompt: A retailer adds a rarely purchased $900 blender to a shelf holding $500 and $300 models, and sales of the $500 model rise sharply. Identify the mechanism:
quiz.answer: A decoy shifts the comparison set
choices: Loss aversion over the price difference.
Hyperbolic discounting of future purchases.
Anchoring on the cheapest listed price.
A decoy shifts the comparison set
quiz.explain: So the middle option starts to look moderate. Choices are made relative to the available set, so introducing an expensive decoy makes a mid-priced option seem like the sensible compromise.

quiz.prompt: A gym offers a monthly pass and a pay-per-visit rate, and most members choose the pass then attend too rarely to break even. Which account explains that choice best?
quiz.answer: People overestimate their own future self-control
choices: People overestimate their own future self-control
Members prefer paying a higher price for the same service
The pass grants access to better equipment in the gym
Members struggle with the arithmetic of the two prices
quiz.explain: Projection bias and over-optimism about future effort explain the pattern documented by DellaVigna and Malmendier in gym contracts.

quiz.prompt: A gamble pays $100 with probability 0.3, $40 with probability 0.5, and nothing otherwise. Compute its expected value in dollars.
quiz.explain: (0.3 x 100) + (0.5 x 40) = 30 + 20 = 50. Expected value is the benchmark against which observed risk preferences are measured.

quiz.prompt: A charity doubles its donations by changing its form so the box reads 'donate $20' by default, with an opt-out. Which mechanism does the change exploit?
quiz.answer: Default effects and the small effort of opting out
choices: Default effects and the small effort of opting out
An income effect from higher household wealth
Loss aversion over the charity's own budget
Bayesian updating about the charity's quality
quiz.explain: Defaults carry enormous weight because opting out costs attention and effort and because the default is read as a recommendation.

quiz.prompt: Two supermarkets sell identical coffee: one lists it at $5.00, the other lists $6.00 with a '$1 off' sign. Sales run higher at the second. Explain the finding using reference points, and give one reason the effect may not last.
quiz.answer: The $6.00 list price supplies a reference point or anchor, so the discount frames the purchase as a gain relative to it, while the flat $5.00 offers no comparison; the effect may fade because regular shoppers learn the usual selling price and adopt that as their reference instead.
quiz.explain: Reference-dependence is the core of prospect theory, and it also explains why permanent sales stop working.

lesson_media.alt: A worked gain-frame choice compares a sure fifty dollars with a fifty-percent chance of one hundred dollars and a fifty-percent chance of zero; both equal fifty dollars in expected value, while a second panel lists how certainty and framing may shift observed choice.
lesson_media.caption: Expected value supplies a normative benchmark in this simplified case. Behavioral evidence tests how actual choices respond to certainty, framing, reference points and loss aversion.

nodes.title: Advanced Logic
nodes.goal: Modal, non-classical logic and their limits.

quiz.prompt: In the standard modal system where □ means 'necessarily' and ◇ means 'possibly,' which pairing correctly expresses the duality between them?
quiz.answer: ◇P is equivalent to ¬□¬P.
quiz.explain: 'Possibly P' means it is not necessary that not-P, so ◇P ≡ ¬□¬P, the standard modal duality.
choices: ◇¬P is equivalent to ¬□¬P.
□P is equivalent to ¬□¬P.
◇P is equivalent to ¬□¬P.
◇P is equivalent to ¬◇¬P.

quiz.prompt: Intuitionistic logic rejects a principle accepted in classical logic. Which principle does it reject, and why?
quiz.answer: Excluded middle (P ∨ ¬P), since a proof of one disjunct is required.
quiz.explain: Intuitionism identifies truth with provability, so it will not assert P ∨ ¬P in general absent a proof of P or of ¬P.
choices: The commutativity of conjunction, because the order of proofs matters.
Non-contradiction, since some statements are both true and false at once.
Modus ponens, because applying it repeatedly leads to contradictions.
Excluded middle (P ∨ ¬P), since a proof of one disjunct is required.

quiz.prompt: A logician writes a first-order theory meant to describe the real numbers uniquely, and a colleague replies that a countable model of that theory must exist. Which conclusion follows about the project?
quiz.answer: First-order axioms cannot pin an uncountable structure down to isomorphism
choices: First-order axioms cannot pin an uncountable structure down to isomorphism
The theory must contain a hidden contradiction
The real numbers turn out to be countable after all
The theory needs infinitely many axioms to succeed
quiz.explain: The downward Löwenheim-Skolem theorem gives a countable model to any satisfiable countable first-order theory, so no such theory characterises the reals up to isomorphism. Skolem's paradox concerns expressive power, not the size of the reals.

quiz.prompt: How many distinct truth-functions of two propositional variables are there? Give the count.
quiz.explain: A two-place truth-function assigns a truth value to each of 4 input rows, giving 2^4 = 16 distinct functions.

quiz.prompt: In a Kripke model, world w accesses only itself, and P is false at w. Evaluate □◇P at w:
quiz.answer: False, since ◇P fails at w.
choices: True, because □ holds vacuously when access is restricted.
True, since reflexive frames validate every modal formula.
False, since ◇P fails at w.
Undefined, because a single world gives no modal information.
quiz.explain: ◇P at w needs an accessible world where P holds; the only accessible world is w, where P is false, so ◇P fails and □◇P fails too.

quiz.prompt: A paraconsistent logician accepts a theory containing both A and ¬A yet denies that everything follows from it. Which classical principle must she give up:
quiz.answer: Ex falso quodlibet (explosion).
choices: Modus ponens.
Ex falso quodlibet (explosion).
The law of non-contradiction as a theorem.
Disjunction introduction as a valid rule.
quiz.explain: Explosion is what makes a single contradiction trivialize a classical theory, so paraconsistent systems block it, typically by restricting disjunctive syllogism.

quiz.prompt: A modal logician models knowledge with an accessibility relation that holds reflexively but not transitively. Which principle fails in that model?
quiz.answer: Knowing implies knowing that one knows
choices: Knowing implies knowing that one knows
Knowing implies truth
Necessity distributes over conditionals
Possibility and necessity remain dual
quiz.explain: Transitivity of accessibility corresponds to the S4 axiom, so dropping it drops positive introspection while reflexivity keeps the factivity axiom.

quiz.prompt: A mathematician proves that a number with a certain property exists by deriving a contradiction from its non-existence, without producing the number. Which school rejects the proof, and on what ground?
quiz.answer: Intuitionists, who require a construction
choices: Intuitionists, who require a construction
Formalists, who reject contradictions of any kind
Classical logicians, who bar reductio arguments
Model theorists, who require a countable model
quiz.explain: Intuitionism rejects the unrestricted law of excluded middle, so a proof by contradiction of an existence claim gives no witness and so no theorem.

quiz.prompt: A first-order language has 2 unary predicates and a domain of 3 named elements. How many distinct assignments of truth values to the atomic sentences of the form P(a) are there?
quiz.explain: 2 predicates x 3 elements gives 6 atomic sentences, and 2 to the power 6 is 64 assignments.

quiz.prompt: A recursively axiomatised theory strong enough for arithmetic proves a sentence expressing its own consistency. Explain, using Gödel's second incompleteness theorem, what follows about that theory.
quiz.answer: The second incompleteness theorem says no such theory can prove its own consistency unless it is inconsistent, so a theory that does prove its own consistency is inconsistent, and by explosion it therefore proves every sentence of its language.
quiz.explain: Gödel's second incompleteness theorem says any consistent, sufficiently powerful axiomatic theory cannot prove its own consistency from within itself — it constrains what a formal system can establish about itself, which is why consistency proofs are given in a stronger metatheory instead.

lesson_media.alt: A possible-world graph has P in accessible world w-one and not-P in w-two, so diamond-P is true while box-P is false; beside it, P and not-P enter one theory but a blocked arrow shows they do not entail unrelated Q.
lesson_media.caption: Modal logic formalizes necessity and possibility through accessibility. Paraconsistent logics alter consequence so contradictions need not make every sentence derivable.

nodes.title: Philosophy of Mind & AI
nodes.goal: Consciousness, the mind-body problem and machine minds.

quiz.prompt: A lab fully explains how the brain discriminates colours, integrates the signal and reports it in speech. A philosopher grants every result and says the central question remains untouched. Which question does she have in mind?
quiz.answer: Why any of that processing feels like something from the inside
choices: Why any of that processing feels like something from the inside
How the brain tells one wavelength from another
Whether colour terms refer to properties of surfaces
How quickly the spoken report follows the stimulus
quiz.explain: Chalmers's hard problem is that a complete functional story answers the 'easy' questions of discrimination, integration and report while leaving unexplained why those processes are accompanied by experience at all.

quiz.prompt: In Searle's Chinese Room, a person who knows no Chinese manipulates symbols by rulebook to produce fluent Chinese replies. Searle uses this to argue what about strong AI?
quiz.answer: Running the right program is not sufficient for genuine understanding.
quiz.explain: The Chinese Room aims to show that symbol manipulation alone yields no understanding, so purely computational syntax cannot constitute semantics.
choices: Understanding requires a biological brain made of neurons specifically.
Computers can never process symbols anywhere near quickly enough.
Running the right program is not sufficient for genuine understanding.
The Turing test remains the correct criterion for having a real mind.

quiz.prompt: The 'knowledge argument' imagines Mary, a scientist who knows every physical fact about color vision but has only seen black and white. When she first sees red, she seems to learn something new. Against which thesis is this aimed?
quiz.answer: Physicalism: the claim that all facts are ultimately physical facts.
quiz.explain: If Mary knew all physical facts yet still learns what red is like, then there are non-physical facts about experience, challenging physicalism.
choices: The identity theory that pain is simply the firing of C-fibers.
Functionalism: the claim that mental states are just functional roles.
Dualism: the claim that the mind is a wholly non-physical substance.
Physicalism: the claim that all facts are ultimately physical facts.

quiz.prompt: A robot reports pain, withdraws from damage, and learns to avoid it, yet a philosopher insists the question of whether it feels anything stays open. Explain which distinction the claim relies on.
quiz.answer: It relies on the gap between functional organisation and phenomenal consciousness: meeting every functional role leaves open whether there is any experience at all.
quiz.explain: Functional and behavioural criteria fix what a system does; the hard question is whether anything it is like accompanies the doing.

quiz.prompt: Two people are behaviourally and functionally identical, but one's colour experiences are systematically swapped relative to the other's. Give the reply most consistent with functionalism:
quiz.answer: It could not happen, since identical functional roles fix mental states.
choices: It could happen, and it shows that mental states are non-physical substances entirely.
It could happen, because experiences depend on the particular neurons in each brain.
It could not happen, since identical functional roles fix mental states.
The question is ill-posed, since colour experiences play no functional role.
quiz.explain: Functionalism identifies mental states with functional roles, so two systems sharing every role cannot differ mentally; inverted-qualia cases are aimed at exactly this.

quiz.prompt: An octopus's problem-solving arises from a nervous system organised very differently from a vertebrate brain, with most neurons in its arms. Say what this pattern supports:
quiz.answer: Multiple realizability
choices: The type-identity theory of mind and brain.
Eliminativism about propositional attitudes.
Cartesian dualism about animal minds.
Multiple realizability
quiz.explain: Since one mental function can be implemented by very different physical systems. Multiple realizability is the standard argument against type-identity theory: the same psychological kind can be realized by distinct physical kinds.

quiz.prompt: An engineer builds a system whose internal states play exactly the causal roles that pain plays in humans, though built from silicon. A functionalist and a type-identity theorist disagree about it. Which claim divides them?
quiz.answer: Whether mental kinds depend on physical composition
choices: Whether mental kinds depend on physical composition
Whether the system behaves as though in pain
Whether silicon conducts electricity efficiently
Whether the engineer intended to create consciousness
quiz.explain: Multiple realisability is the crux: functionalism individuates mental states by causal role, type identity by physical type.

quiz.prompt: A patient reports no visual experience yet reliably points to lights in the blind field. Which philosophical use of blindsight carries most force?
quiz.answer: It separates access to information from conscious experience
choices: It separates access to information from conscious experience
It shows that visual experience causes nothing at all
It proves the hard problem has now been solved
It demonstrates that reports track experience exactly
quiz.explain: Blindsight is the standard empirical wedge between access consciousness and phenomenal consciousness in Block's distinction.

quiz.prompt: A researcher runs a Turing-style test with 5 judges, and the machine must be judged human by more than half of them. State the minimum number of judges it must convince.
quiz.explain: More than 2.5 means 3 judges. The arbitrariness of such thresholds is itself one of the standard criticisms of the test as a criterion for mind.

quiz.prompt: A company claims its language model has feelings because it says so when questioned. Set out why the report carries little evidential weight, and what kind of evidence would carry more.
quiz.answer: The model's training optimises it to produce text people judge apt, so a self-report about feelings is exactly what the training would produce whether or not anything is felt, making the report nearly uninformative; stronger evidence would have to come from architecture and behaviour that goes beyond the training signal, such as costly avoidance, spontaneous trade-offs, or integration across tasks the training never rewarded.
quiz.explain: The general point is that a signal produced by the very process being tested cannot discriminate the hypotheses at issue.

lesson_media.alt: A reciprocal network places an AI system reporting pain at the center and connects observable behavior, functional organization, physical implementation and subjective experience, with the last marked as not settled by performance alone.
lesson_media.caption: Behavioral competence, functional organization, physical mechanism and subjective experience are distinct targets. Evidence about one constrains but may not settle claims about the others.

nodes.title: Philosophy of Language
nodes.goal: Meaning, reference and truth in language.

quiz.prompt: Frege distinguished the 'sense' (Sinn) from the 'reference' (Bedeutung) of an expression to explain how 'the morning star is the evening star' can be informative. How does the distinction do this?
quiz.answer: Both terms refer to Venus but present it under different senses.
quiz.explain: Sharing a reference but differing in sense lets the identity statement convey new information rather than being a trivial tautology.
choices: The two terms have different references but exactly the same sense.
The terms are both meaningless because stars are not really planets.
Both terms refer to Venus but present it under different senses.
Reference is subjective while sense is objective and fixed for all.

quiz.prompt: Someone claims that 'Aristotle' merely abbreviates 'the greatest pupil of Plato'. A critic asks us to consider a world in which that man died in infancy and another pupil earned the title. Which conclusion does the critic draw?
quiz.answer: The name still picks out the same man; the description does not
choices: The name still picks out the same man; the description does not
Both the name and the description pick out whoever earned the title
The name would then refer to nobody at all
The description fixes the reference in every possible world
quiz.explain: A rigid designator picks out the same individual in every world where that individual exists, which is why names behave differently from the descriptions we happen to associate with them.

quiz.prompt: The later Wittgenstein's slogan 'meaning is use' and his private-language argument together suggest what about linguistic meaning?
quiz.answer: Meaning rests on public rule-following, so a private language is impossible.
quiz.explain: For the later Wittgenstein, meaning arises from shared practices and rule-following, which undermines the coherence of an essentially private language.
choices: Meaning rests on public rule-following, so a private language is impossible.
Only formal logical languages can ever carry genuine determinate meaning.
Meaning is a private mental image each speaker inspects introspectively.
Words mean whatever their dictionary definition states, independently of use.

quiz.prompt: Asked for a reference letter, a professor writes only 'Mr X has excellent handwriting and was always punctual.' Explain in Gricean terms how the letter communicates more than it says.
quiz.answer: It flouts the maxim of quantity by supplying less relevant information than the occasion demands, generating a conversational implicature that the professor has nothing good to say about the candidate's ability.
quiz.explain: Implicature arises when a speaker visibly violates a conversational maxim while remaining cooperative, forcing the hearer to infer the unstated point.

quiz.prompt: Someone utters 'The present King of France is bald' and denies both that it is true and that its negation is true. On Russell's theory of descriptions, diagnose the sentence:
quiz.answer: It is false, since it asserts an existence that fails.
choices: It is neither true nor false, because it suffers a failure of presupposition.
It is true, since no French king happens to have any hair on his head.
It is false, since it asserts an existence that fails.
It is meaningless, since a term without a bearer fails to express anything.
quiz.explain: Russell analyses the description as an existence claim conjoined with uniqueness and predication, so with no king the whole sentence comes out false.

quiz.prompt: Uttered by different speakers in different places, 'I am here now' comes out true whenever it is uttered, yet expresses a different proposition each time. Say what this shows about indexicals:
quiz.answer: Their character is a fixed rule that yields different content in each context of utterance.
choices: They are ambiguous between several stable meanings.
They are rigid designators of abstract objects.
They have content but no linguistic meaning.
Their character is a fixed rule that yields different content in each context of utterance.
quiz.explain: Kaplan separates character, the context-invariant meaning, from content, what is expressed on an occasion; indexicals have stable character and shifting content.

quiz.prompt: A speaker says 'Some of the students passed' while knowing that all of them did. The statement holds true, yet the hearer feels misled. Which analysis fits?
quiz.answer: A quantity implicature got flouted, leaving truth conditions intact
choices: A quantity implicature got flouted, leaving truth conditions intact
The sentence expressed a straightforward falsehood
The word 'some' changed its meaning in that context
The hearer simply misheard the utterance
quiz.explain: Grice's maxim of quantity generates the implicature that not all passed; it is cancellable and does not belong to what the sentence strictly says.

quiz.prompt: Two communities apply the word 'water' to chemically different liquids that look and behave alike. Putnam argues their words differ in reference. Which principle drives the argument?
quiz.answer: Reference gets fixed by the external substance, not by what speakers think
choices: Reference gets fixed by the external substance, not by what speakers think
Meaning depends on the mental images that a speaker associates with the word
Names abbreviate whichever descriptions the speaker happens to accept of them
Words refer to whatever a community intends them to
quiz.explain: Twin Earth motivates semantic externalism: meanings, in Putnam's phrase, are not in the head.

quiz.prompt: A toy grammar forms sentences by choosing a subject noun, a transitive verb and an object noun, with subject and object required to be different. Given 3 nouns and 2 verbs, how many sentences can be formed?
quiz.explain: 3 subjects x 2 verbs x 2 remaining objects = 12. Compositional semantics explains how finite resources yield systematically many meanings.

quiz.prompt: A witness says 'the man in the brown coat took it', and it turns out nobody in the room wore brown, though everyone knew which man was meant. Explain the tension between Russell's and Donnellan's treatments.
quiz.answer: On Russell's analysis the definite description carries an existence and uniqueness condition that nothing satisfies, so what the witness said comes out false; Donnellan distinguishes a referential use in which the description merely helps the audience identify a man the speaker had in mind, so the speaker can say something true of him despite the misdescription.
quiz.explain: Donnellan's referential-attributive distinction is usually framed as a challenge to whether Russell's theory captures speaker meaning.

lesson_media.alt: Two context panels contain the identical sentence I am here now; arrows map I, here and now to Amina, Cape Town and 09:00 in one context and to Bo, Nairobi and 10:00 in the other.
lesson_media.caption: Indexicals show why sentence type alone does not fix reference or truth conditions. Speaker, place and time supply context-sensitive values.

nodes.title: Political & Social Philosophy
nodes.goal: Justice, power and the good society, rigorously.

quiz.prompt: A committee of school heads must set a funding rule, and each of them knows which school they run. A reformer proposes that they settle the rule before learning their assignment. Which effect on the rule does the proposal aim at?
quiz.answer: It blocks rules tailored to their own position
choices: It blocks rules tailored to their own position
It ensures the wealthiest schools accept the outcome
It replaces bargaining power with expert judgement
It makes the rule easier for parents to understand
quiz.explain: This applies the veil of ignorance locally: removing knowledge of one's own position turns self-interested choice into a test of what one could accept from any position. Critics ask whether parties stripped of that knowledge have enough information to choose at all.

quiz.prompt: Nozick objects to patterned theories of distributive justice with his 'Wilt Chamberlain' argument. What is its core claim?
quiz.answer: Voluntary transfers from a just distribution yield a just inequality.
quiz.explain: Nozick argues that upholding any fixed pattern of distribution would require continually blocking voluntary exchanges, conflicting with individual liberty.
choices: The state should redistribute wealth to maximize total happiness.
Equality of outcome is the only distribution that could ever be just.
Talented people deserve more because their talents are morally earned.
Voluntary transfers from a just distribution yield a just inequality.

quiz.prompt: Marx's theory of history holds that under capitalism workers are 'alienated.' Which best captures his concept of alienation?
quiz.answer: Workers are estranged from their products, their labor, and themselves.
quiz.explain: For Marx, alienation is structural: lacking ownership of the means and products of production estranges workers from their labor and their species-being, not merely a feeling of loneliness.
choices: Workers lack the education needed to understand modern economics.
Workers dislike their coworkers and feel socially lonely at the factory.
Workers are simply paid too little to afford the goods that they make.
Workers are estranged from their products, their labor, and themselves.

quiz.prompt: Rawls's difference principle ranks arrangements by the position of the worst-off group. Arrangement A yields incomes 10, 40 and 90; arrangement B yields 25, 30 and 55. Give the worst-off income under the arrangement the principle selects.
quiz.explain: The principle compares the worst-off positions, 10 versus 25, and selects B despite its lower total, so the answer is 25.

quiz.prompt: A state removes every legal barrier to university entry but leaves fees that few poor students can pay. Berlin's distinction is invoked against it. State the complaint most precisely:
quiz.answer: Negative liberty is secured while positive liberty is not.
choices: Negative liberty has been violated, since a legal prohibition remains in force.
Positive liberty has been violated by opening entry to applicants.
Negative liberty is secured while positive liberty is not.
The distinction does not apply, because fees are set by universities and not the state.
quiz.explain: Removing interference secures negative liberty; whether people have the means to exercise the opportunity is a question of positive liberty.

quiz.prompt: Two societies have identical income distributions, but in one, women are barred from working outside the home. Sen argues an income-based measure misses something. Name what it misses:
quiz.answer: Capabilities: the real freedoms people have to act.
choices: Gross domestic product per person.
Capabilities: the real freedoms people have to act.
The utility each person derives from consumption.
The historical entitlements standing behind each holding.
quiz.explain: Sen's capability approach evaluates what people are actually able to do and be, which income alone can conceal.

quiz.prompt: A city allocates scarce transplant organs by lottery among all medically eligible patients. A critic objects that this ignores who would benefit most. Which value conflict does the objection expose?
quiz.answer: Equal respect for persons against maximising outcomes
choices: Equal respect for persons against maximising outcomes
Procedural fairness against legal formality
Liberty against collective security
Desert against contractual obligation
quiz.explain: Lotteries express the claim that each person's stake counts equally and refuse to rank lives by expected benefit, which is precisely what the critic wants done.

quiz.prompt: A firm relocates and a town loses most of its jobs, though every individual contract held to its terms. A political philosopher argues that justice concerns more than the contracts. Which claim best supports the argument?
quiz.answer: Basic structures distribute burdens that no single contract records
choices: Basic structures distribute burdens that no single contract records
Contracts require government approval before they can bind anyone
Individuals owe nothing whatever to strangers
Firms hold legal personality and therefore bear duties of their own
quiz.explain: Rawls locates the primary subject of justice in the basic structure rather than in individual transactions, so a series of fair trades can still produce an unjust distribution.

quiz.prompt: A society has five groups with incomes 10, 20, 30, 40 and 100. Compute the share of total income held by the richest group, as a percentage.
quiz.explain: The total is 200, so 100/200 is 50%. Top-share measures like this capture concentration that an average or even a Gini can obscure.

quiz.prompt: A state guarantees a right to vote while drawing districts so that one party's votes reliably translate into more seats. Explain why formal equality and political equality come apart here, and name the criterion a critic would apply.
quiz.answer: Each citizen holds a formally equal vote, yet the effective weight of a vote in producing representation differs by district, so equality of outcome in political influence fails while equality of legal status holds; a critic applies a criterion of equal effective influence, asking whether equal numbers of votes yield roughly equal representation.
quiz.explain: The criticism is structural: it concerns how votes map onto power, and it can be stated without settling which party the districting favours.

lesson_media.alt: A reciprocal network places an affordable-housing policy at the center and connects distribution of benefits and burdens, recognition and status, democratic procedure, and power over land and agenda-setting.
lesson_media.caption: Political philosophy evaluates not only who receives resources, but also status, decision procedures and the power that shapes available choices.

nodes.title: Enduring Questions
nodes.goal: The problems philosophy has not solved, and why.
articles: List of unsolved problems in philosophy

quiz.prompt: Many 'unsolved problems in philosophy,' such as the problem of consciousness or the nature of moral facts, share a feature that makes them resist the methods that settle empirical science. Which feature is it?
quiz.answer: They turn on conceptual and normative questions no experiment settles.
quiz.explain: Enduring philosophical problems frequently concern meanings, values, and frameworks rather than measurable facts, so empirical testing alone cannot settle them.
choices: They have in fact all been solved but the solutions are kept secret.
They simply lack enough research funding for the necessary experiments.
They turn on conceptual and normative questions no experiment settles.
They are trivial pseudo-questions with obviously correct answers.

quiz.prompt: A philosopher argues that even a technologically perfect future, free of disease and scarcity, would still leave the 'meaning of life' question open. What is the strongest reason this could be true?
quiz.answer: Meaningfulness is evaluative, and material abundance cannot settle it.
quiz.explain: Meaning concerns what is worth caring about and pursuing, an evaluative matter that solving material problems does not by itself resolve.
choices: Future technology will certainly fail one day, so scarcity would return.
Meaning is identical to pleasure, so abundance would supply it fully.
The question is incoherent and therefore admits of no possible answer.
Meaningfulness is evaluative, and material abundance cannot settle it.

quiz.prompt: In the ethics of artificial intelligence, the 'value alignment problem' is considered genuinely hard. Which formulation best captures why?
quiz.answer: Human values are contested and hard to state, yet must be specified.
quiz.explain: Alignment is hard partly because human values resist complete, uncontroversial specification, so encoding them faithfully into a capable system is deeply difficult.
choices: Machines cannot process ethical words such as 'good' or 'fair' at all.
Human values are contested and hard to state, yet must be specified.
Only governments, and never engineers, are permitted to define values.
Current AI systems run far too slowly to act on any human values.

quiz.prompt: Some philosophers argue that the problem of consciousness may be 'cognitively closed' to human minds. Explain the claim and one reason it is hard to establish.
quiz.answer: The claim is that our cognitive faculties may be constitutively unable to grasp the solution, as a dog cannot grasp arithmetic; it is hard to establish because arguing that a problem is closed to us seems to require some grasp of what a solution would involve.
quiz.explain: Cognitive closure treats the difficulty as a fact about our minds rather than about the world, which makes the thesis notoriously hard to argue from the inside.

quiz.prompt: A researcher proposes settling the free-will debate with a brain-imaging experiment. A philosopher replies that no scan could settle it. Give the strongest version of that reply:
quiz.answer: The parties disagree over what would count as freedom, so the dispute is partly conceptual and no measurement resolves it.
choices: Brain scanners lack the spatial and temporal resolution needed to observe individual decisions as they are actually being made.
Free will belongs to religion rather than to inquiry.
Experiments on human subjects are forbidden here.
The parties disagree over what would count as freedom, so the dispute is partly conceptual and no measurement resolves it.
quiz.explain: When rival positions attach different truth conditions to the term, data cannot adjudicate until the concept is fixed.

quiz.prompt: Asked why philosophy has not converged on answers the way chemistry has, a philosopher notes that questions which do get settled tend to be renamed as sciences. Say what this observation implies:
quiz.answer: Philosophy retains the residue of unsettled questions.
choices: Philosophical questions are pseudo-questions that admit of no answers at all.
Chemistry and philosophy are in fact studying exactly the same subject matter.
Philosophy retains the residue of unsettled questions.
Progress is impossible in philosophy because its methods are fundamentally flawed.
quiz.explain: If solved problems migrate out of the field, the visible remainder is selected for difficulty, which makes apparent stagnation misleading.

quiz.prompt: A neuroscientist proposes to settle whether other animals have conscious experience by measuring a neural signature validated on humans. Which objection cuts deepest?
quiz.answer: The signature's validation presupposes reports animals cannot give
choices: The signature's validation presupposes reports animals cannot give
Animal brains contain far fewer neurons overall
The measurement disturbs the animal's behaviour
Consciousness varies across the day even in humans
quiz.explain: The measure was calibrated against verbal report, so exporting it to creatures who cannot report begs the question it was meant to answer.

quiz.prompt: Two research groups define 'intelligence' differently and then disagree about whether a system has it, without disputing any measurement. Which diagnosis of the disagreement fits best?
quiz.answer: The dispute turns on the concept rather than the evidence
choices: The dispute turns on the concept rather than the evidence
One group must have miscalibrated its instruments
Gathering more data will resolve the disagreement
The disagreement concerns terminology and so lacks interest
quiz.explain: Conceptual disputes are not settled by data, but they are not merely verbal either: which concept to adopt has consequences for what gets studied and regulated.

quiz.prompt: A survey of 1,000 philosophers reports that 56% lean toward one view on a contested question and 27% toward its rival. How many more respondents lean toward the first view?
quiz.explain: 560 - 270 = 290. Persistent splits of this kind are the datum that theories of philosophical disagreement have to explain.

quiz.prompt: A committee must decide whether an AI system deserves moral consideration without resolving the hard problem of consciousness. Set out a decision procedure that respects the uncertainty, and one cost of adopting it.
quiz.answer: Treat it as a decision under moral uncertainty: assign credences to the system having morally relevant experience, weigh the expected moral cost of error in each direction, and adopt safeguards proportional to that credence and to the stakes; the cost is that a low but non-zero credence can generate large obligations, and that systems designed to elicit sympathy can inflate the credence itself.
quiz.explain: Expected-value reasoning under moral uncertainty is the standard framework here, and its vulnerability to manipulated inputs is the standard objection.

lesson_media.alt: Four evidence streams—neural and behavioral data, linguistic practice, moral disagreement and machine behavior—converge on a method of argument, models and counterexamples, then lead to qualified constraints rather than a box labeled solved.
lesson_media.caption: Enduring philosophical problems persist because evidence underdetermines key concepts or values, not because inquiry makes no progress. Arguments can rule out answers and sharpen what remains.
